verse.text: Since many have undertaken to compile an account of the events that have been fulfilled among us,

note.traditional: most surely believed (KJV); fulfilled or accomplished (most modern versions)

verse.note: The verb can mean to bring something to completion or to convince someone fully. Most scholars take it here of events brought to completion, with the overtone that God's purposes were being carried out in them. The older rendering ‘most surely believed’ takes it in the second sense.

verse.text: just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and became servants of the word,
it seemed good to me also, having followed everything carefully from the start, to write it out for you in order, most excellent Theophilus,
so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.
In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. His wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
verse.note: The priests were organised into twenty-four hereditary divisions (1 Chronicles 24), of which Abijah's was the eighth. Each division served at the temple for a week at a time, twice a year. Because there were many priests, duties such as offering the incense were assigned by lot, as in verse 9.

verse.text: Both of them were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and righteous requirements of the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek word belongs to the same family as ‘righteous’ earlier in the verse, and the rendering keeps that link visible. In the Septuagint it regularly refers to God's statutes, so ‘ordinances’ is not wrong. Greek has a single word-family where English divides between righteous/just and righteousness/justice.

verse.text: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were far along in their days.
Now it happened that, while he was serving as priest before God in the turn of his division,
he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense.
verse.note: Greek distinguishes the sanctuary building itself, which only priests entered, from the whole temple complex with its courts, for which a different word is used. The people praying ‘outside’ in verse 10 are in the courts, still within the temple in the wider sense. Most English versions use ‘temple’ for both words.

verse.text: The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of the incense offering.
Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the altar of incense.
Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to name him John.

text.q: You will have joy and delight, and many will rejoice at his birth,
for he will be great before the Lord. He is never to drink wine or beer, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.

verse.note: The Greek word is borrowed from a Semitic term for fermented drinks other than grape wine, chiefly grain-based beer. ‘Strong drink’ now suggests distilled spirits, which were unknown in antiquity; some versions use ‘other fermented drink’. The wording echoes the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6:3 and the instructions about Samson in Judges 13.

text.q: He will turn many of the children of Israel back to the Lord their God.

And he will go on before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.”

verse.text: Zechariah said to the angel, “How will I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is far along in her days.”
The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands before God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.

text.q: And look, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their proper time.”

verse.text: Meanwhile the people were waiting for Zechariah and were amazed at how long he was staying in the sanctuary.
When he came out he could not speak to them, and they realised that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He kept making signs to them and remained mute.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean mute, deaf, or both. Verse 20 mentions only the loss of speech, and the rendering follows that. But verse 62, where people make signs to Zechariah, suggests he could not hear either.

verse.text: When the days of his service were completed, he went back to his home.
After those days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she kept herself hidden for five months, saying,

text.q: “This is what the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked upon me to take away my disgrace among people.”

verse.text: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town in Galilee named Nazareth,
to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. The virgin’s name was Mary.
He came in to her and said, “Greetings, favoured one! The Lord is with you.”

note.traditional: Hail, full of grace; Hail, thou that art highly favoured

verse.note: The first word was the ordinary Greek greeting, though it literally means ‘rejoice’, and some scholars hear that sense here. The second is a passive form meaning one to whom favour has been shown, and it chimes in sound with the greeting. ‘Full of grace’ comes from the Latin version; most modern translations render it much as here.

verse.text: But she was deeply troubled at his words and pondered what kind of greeting this might be.
The angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God.

text.q: And look, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus.
He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David,
and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will have no end.”

verse.text: Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I have not slept with a man?”

note.term: since I have not slept with a man
note.traditional: seeing I know not a man; since I am a virgin

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘since I do not know a man’, using the biblical idiom in which ‘know’ refers to sexual intercourse. The present tense describes her current state. The rendering replaces the Hebrew idiom with an equivalent English one.

verse.text: The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be called holy, Son of God.

note.term: will be called holy, Son of God
note.traditional: that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in two ways: ‘the child to be born will be called holy, Son of God’ or ‘the holy one to be born will be called Son of God’. The rendering follows the punctuation of the Greek edition translated here. Scholars are divided, and the difference in meaning is slight.

text.q: And look, your relative Elizabeth has herself conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren.
For no word from God will be powerless.”

note.term: no word from God will be powerless
note.traditional: For nothing will be impossible with God

verse.note: The Greek noun means ‘word’ but, under Hebrew influence, can also mean ‘thing’. The sentence echoes Genesis 18:14 in the Septuagint, where it is usually understood as ‘thing’, and most versions render accordingly here. This translation keeps ‘word’ because the text has ‘from God’ and because Mary takes up the same noun in the next verse; both readings are defensible.

verse.text: Mary said, “Here I am, the Lord’s slave. May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel left her.
verse.note: This is the ordinary Greek word for a female slave, and most versions soften it to ‘servant’ or ‘handmaid’. In the Septuagint, people use it of themselves when speaking humbly to God, as Hannah does in 1 Samuel 1:11, which Mary's song echoes in verse 48. It expresses belonging wholly to a master and readiness to obey, not degradation.

verse.text: In those days Mary set out and went in haste to the hill country, to a town of Judah,
and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leapt in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
She cried out in a loud voice and said, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!

text.q: And why should this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
For look, when the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leapt with delight.
And blessed is she who believed that what was spoken to her from the Lord would be fulfilled.”

note.term: blessed is she who believed that
note.traditional: blessed is she who believed that (or: for) there would be a fulfilment

verse.note: The Greek conjunction can mean ‘that’ or ‘because’, so the sentence may also be read ‘blessed is she who believed, for what was spoken to her will be fulfilled’. Most translations choose ‘that’. The word for ‘blessed’ here is a different Greek word from the one in verse 42: this one pronounces someone to be in an enviable state, the other speaks of being blessed by God.

verse.text: And Mary said, “My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord,

text.q: and my spirit delights in God my Saviour,
for he has taken notice of the lowliness of his slave. For look, from now on all generations will call me blessed,
for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name,
and his mercy is on those who fear him, from generation to generation.
He has done a mighty deed with his arm; he has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts.
He has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the lowly;
he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.
He has helped Israel his servant, remembering mercy,
just as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.”

verse.text: Mary stayed with her about three months and then returned to her home.
Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.
Her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were going to call him Zechariah, after his father.
But his mother spoke up and said, “No! He is to be called John.”
They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who is called by that name.”
So they made signs to his father, asking what he would want him to be called.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “John is his name.” And they were all amazed.
At once his mouth was opened and his tongue set free, and he began to speak, blessing God.
Fear came over all who lived around them, and all these things were talked about throughout the hill country of Judea.
All who heard them stored them in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For indeed the hand of the Lord was with him.
His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying,

text.q: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited his people and worked redemption for them,
and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant,

verse.note: In the Hebrew Scriptures an animal's horn is a standing image of strength, and Psalm 132:17 speaks of God making a horn grow for David. The phrase means a powerful deliverer, here one from David's royal line.

text.q: just as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old:
salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant,
the oath he swore to Abraham our father, to grant us
that we, rescued from the hand of enemies, might serve him without fear
in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
to give his people knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins,
because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high will visit us,

verse.note: Some of the earliest manuscripts have the future tense, which the Greek edition translated here adopts. The majority of later manuscripts have the past tense, matching verse 68, and the King James Version follows them. Most modern editions prefer the future.

note.traditional: the dayspring from on high; the rising sun

verse.note: The Greek word means a rising, usually of the sun or a star, and the image of light in verse 79 supports ‘dawn’. In the Septuagint the same word also translates the Hebrew for ‘branch’ or ‘shoot’, a title for the coming Davidic king (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). Many scholars think both associations are in play.

text.q: to shine on those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.”

verse.text: The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole inhabited world should be registered.
(This was the first registration, made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.)

note.term: when Quirinius was governor of Syria
note.traditional: when Quirinius was governor of Syria

verse.note: Quirinius is known to have become governor of Syria in AD 6 and to have held a census of Judea then, about ten years after the death of Herod the Great, in whose reign Luke 1:5 and Matthew place Jesus’ birth. Proposed solutions include an earlier, otherwise unattested term of office for Quirinius, or translating ‘this registration was before Quirinius governed Syria’, which most grammarians find strained. The rendering here is the natural sense of the Greek; the historical difficulty is real and unresolved.

verse.text: And everyone went to be registered, each to his own town.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the town of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David,
verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures ‘the city of David’ normally means the fortress of Zion in Jerusalem. Luke applies the phrase to Bethlehem, the village David came from, linking the birth to the hope for a ruler from David’s line. The same Greek word is used here for Nazareth and Bethlehem and is rendered ‘town’ throughout, since neither was a city in the modern sense.

verse.text: to be registered with Mary, who was betrothed to him and was pregnant.
While they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth,
and she gave birth to her firstborn son. She swaddled him and laid him in a manger, because there was no space for them in the guest room.
verse.note: The Greek word means a place to stay and is not the usual term for a commercial inn, for which Luke uses a different word in 10:34; in 22:11 he uses this word for the guest room of the Last Supper. Many scholars therefore picture a crowded guest room or lodging in a private house, with the baby laid where the animals were fed. The traditional ‘inn’ remains possible, and the exact kind of lodging cannot be settled.

verse.text: In the same region there were shepherds living out in the fields and keeping the night watches over their flock.
An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
The angel said to them, “Do not be afraid; for look, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people:

text.q: today in the town of David a Savior has been born for you, who is the Messiah, the Lord.

verse.note: The Greek christos here is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, so it is rendered ‘Messiah’, as in several modern translations; ‘Christ’ is kept where the word works as a name. The pairing of the two titles without articles is unusual and could also be read ‘an anointed Lord’. Verse 26 has the more common expression, ‘the Lord’s Messiah’.

text.q: And this will be the sign for you: you will find a baby swaddled and lying in a manger.”

verse.text: Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying,
verse.note: ‘Host’ is an old English word for an army, and the Greek word is an ordinary term for a military force. The Septuagint uses the phrase for the ranks of heavenly beings that attend God. With ‘host’ a modern reader can miss that it is an army that announces peace.

text.q: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people with whom he is pleased.”

note.term: among people with whom he is pleased

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read ‘people of good pleasure’, while later manuscripts differ by one letter and give the familiar ‘peace, good will toward men’. Most scholars accept the earlier reading. Similar Hebrew and Aramaic phrases in the Dead Sea Scrolls indicate that it refers to people on whom God’s favor rests, not to people who have good will.

verse.text: When the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds began saying to one another, “Let us go over to Bethlehem, then, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
They came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger.
When they had seen it, they made known the word that had been spoken to them about this child.
And all who heard were amazed at what the shepherds told them.
But Mary treasured all these things, pondering them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, just as it had been told to them.
When eight days were completed for his circumcision, he was given the name Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
When the days of their purification were completed according to the law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord,
verse.note: Leviticus 12 prescribes purification for the mother alone, forty days after the birth of a son; the consecration of a firstborn son (Exodus 13) was a separate obligation. Luke’s ‘their’ is unexpected and has been taken to mean Mary and Joseph, or mother and child, or to be a loose combination of the two rites; a few manuscripts and versions alter it to ‘his’ or ‘her’. The offering of two birds in verse 24 is the one Leviticus allows for those who cannot afford a lamb.

verse.text: as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,”
and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: the same adjective can be translated ‘righteous’ or ‘just’, and the related noun ‘righteousness’ or ‘justice’. Here it describes a person who lives rightly before God, and the traditional ‘righteous’ is kept.

verse.text: It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.
Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what the custom of the law required,
Simeon himself took him in his arms and blessed God and said,

text.q: “Now you are releasing your slave, Master, according to your word, in peace;

verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, and Simeon addresses God with the word for a slave’s owner (‘Master’, often rendered ‘Lord’). The verb means to release or dismiss and was also used of letting someone die. Most translations have ‘servant’ and ‘let depart’. In the Septuagint, ‘slave’ of God is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David.

text.q: for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you have prepared in the sight of all the peoples,
a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for your people Israel.”

verse.note: The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then rendered ‘Gentiles’. It is one word in Greek, translated ‘nation’ or ‘Gentiles’ according to sense. Here it is set beside ‘your people Israel’, echoing Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6.

verse.text: His father and mother were amazed at what was being said about him.
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, “Look, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that is spoken against—

text.q: and a sword will pass through your own soul too—so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

verse.text: There was also Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was far advanced in years, having lived with a husband for seven years after her marriage,
and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She never left the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayers night and day.

note.term: as a widow until she was eighty-four
note.traditional: a widow of about fourscore and four years

verse.note: The Greek can mean either that Anna lived as a widow up to the age of eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years, which would make her over a hundred. Most translations take the first reading, as here. The second is grammatically possible.

verse.text: Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to God and kept speaking about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
When they had carried out everything required by the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town, Nazareth.
The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favor of God was upon him.
Every year his parents went to Jerusalem for the festival of Passover.
When he was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the festival,
and when the days were over and they started back, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.
Assuming he was in the traveling party, they went a day’s journey and then began looking for him among their relatives and acquaintances.
When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, looking for him.
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
All who heard him were astonished at his understanding and his answers.
When his parents saw him they were astounded, and his mother said to him, “Child, why have you done this to us? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish.”
He said to them, “Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘in the things of my Father’, with no noun expressed. Most modern scholars take it as an idiom for being at someone’s house, which suits the setting in the temple. The older rendering ‘about my Father’s business’ is also possible, as is ‘among those who belong to my Father’.

verse.text: But they did not understand the word he spoke to them.
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. His mother kept all these things in her heart.
And Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and people.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either bodily height or age and maturity. ‘Stature’ follows the traditional reading; several modern translations have ‘in years’ instead. The verse echoes the description of the boy Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26.

verse.text: In the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
verse.note: A tetrarch was a dependent prince ruling part of a kingdom under Roman authority, ranking below a king. This Herod is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, whose territory was divided among his sons at his death. The fifteenth year of Tiberius is usually placed around AD 28 or 29, though the exact reckoning is disputed.

verse.text: during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, a word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

note.term: during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verse.note: The Greek has 'high priest' in the singular with two names. Only one man held the office at a time; Caiaphas was the serving high priest in this period. Annas, his father-in-law, had been deposed by the Romans years earlier but kept great influence, and he is still called high priest elsewhere in the New Testament.

verse.text: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance', which in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, as John's practical instructions in verses 10–14 show. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.

text.q: Every ravine will be filled in, and every mountain and hill will be made low; the crooked places will become straight, and the rough ways smooth roads;
and all flesh will see the salvation of God.’”

verse.text: So he would say to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

text.q: Produce, then, fruits worthy of turning back, and do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.
Already the axe is lying at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

verse.text: And the crowds kept asking him, “What then should we do?”
He would answer them, “Whoever has two tunics must share with the one who has none, and whoever has food must do the same.”
Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what should we do?”
He said to them, “Collect nothing more than what you have been ordered to.”
Soldiers too were asking him, “And we, what should we do?” He said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or false charges, and be content with your pay.”
As the people were waiting expectantly, and all were wondering in their hearts about John, whether he might perhaps be the Messiah,
verse.note: The Greek word means 'anointed one' and here is a title for the king Israel was expecting, not a name. 'Messiah' conveys that the crowd is asking about an office. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels where the title itself is under discussion, keeping 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

verse.text: John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but one who is stronger than I am is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not fit to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

note.term: with the Holy Spirit and fire

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean 'with' or 'in', so 'in the Holy Spirit and fire' is equally possible. It is also disputed whether 'fire' describes purification of those who receive the Spirit, or judgment on those who do not, as the burning chaff in the next verse might suggest. Some interpreters see both.

text.q: His winnowing shovel is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

verse.text: So, with many other exhortations as well, he proclaimed good news to the people.
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been rebuked by him about Herodias, his brother’s wife, and about all the evil things that Herod had done,
added this also to them all: he locked John up in prison.
Now when all the people had been baptized, and when Jesus too had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit came down on him in bodily form, like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”

note.term: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

verse.note: A few witnesses, chiefly Codex Bezae, the Old Latin, and several early Christian writers, read instead 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you', quoting Psalm 2:7. The great majority of manuscripts have the reading translated here, and most editors prefer it, though some scholars argue the other reading is original. The Greek could also be punctuated 'my Son, the Beloved'.

verse.text: Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began his work, being the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, son of Heli,
verse.note: The Greek says only 'when beginning', without stating what he began. Most interpreters take it as the start of his public activity, and 'his work' is supplied to complete the English. An older reading takes it with the age: 'was beginning to be about thirty years old'.

The phrase looks back to the account of Jesus' birth in the first two chapters, where Joseph is not his natural father. Luke's genealogy runs backwards from Jesus to Adam and differs from Matthew's between Joseph and David, tracing the line through David's son Nathan, not Solomon. Explanations have been proposed since antiquity, including that one list gives Mary's line or a legal line of descent, but none is certain.

verse.text: son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Melchi, son of Jannai, son of Joseph,
son of Mattathias, son of Amos, son of Nahum, son of Esli, son of Naggai,
son of Maath, son of Mattathias, son of Semein, son of Josech, son of Joda,
son of Joanan, son of Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, son of Neri,
son of Melchi, son of Addi, son of Cosam, son of Elmadam, son of Er,
son of Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Matthat, son of Levi,
verse.note: The Greek name here is identical to the name 'Jesus'; both represent the Hebrew name Joshua. English translations conventionally write 'Joshua' for this ancestor to distinguish him, though older versions have 'Jose' or 'Jesus'.

verse.text: son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam, son of Eliakim,
son of Melea, son of Menna, son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David,
son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Sala, son of Nahshon,
verse.note: The manuscripts vary over several names in this part of the list. The edition translated here reads 'Sala' where many manuscripts have 'Salmon', the form found in Matthew and in Ruth, and it spells the name before Boaz in a way that still plainly refers to Obed. Copyists often adjusted unfamiliar names toward the Old Testament forms.

verse.text: son of Amminadab, son of Admin, son of Arni, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah,

note.term: son of Admin, son of Arni

verse.note: This is among the most confused points in the genealogy's manuscript tradition. Many manuscripts read 'son of Aram' (the Ram of Ruth 4:19 and Matthew 1:3–4) in place of these two names, and others have further combinations. The names Admin and Arni are otherwise unknown, which is why many editors judge them original and the alternatives to be corrections.

verse.text: son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, son of Terah, son of Nahor,
son of Serug, son of Reu, son of Peleg, son of Eber, son of Shelah,
son of Cainan, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, son of Lamech,
verse.note: This Cainan, placed between Arphaxad and Shelah, appears in the Greek Septuagint version of Genesis 10–11 but not in the Hebrew text. Luke's list follows the Greek Scriptures used by his readers. A different Cainan, called Kenan in English Old Testaments, appears in verse 37.

verse.text: son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Jared, son of Mahalalel, son of Cainan,
son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam, son of God.
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was being led by the Spirit in the wilderness
for forty days, being tested by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were over he was hungry.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both testing and tempting, and most translations have 'tempted' here. 'Tested' is used because the scene echoes Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each time from that part of Deuteronomy. It also keeps the link with verse 12, where a compound of the same verb means putting God to the test, and with the related noun in verse 13. The devil's aim is certainly to make Jesus fail, so 'tempted' is not wrong.

verse.text: The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘A person will not live on bread alone.’”
Then, leading him up, he showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time,
verse.note: Luke does not use the general word for 'world' here but a term meaning the inhabited earth, which in his day often meant in practice the Roman empire and its neighbours. Most translations simply have 'the world'. The parallel in Matthew uses the more general word.

verse.text: and the devil said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.

text.q: So if you will bow in worship before me, it will all be yours.”

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”
Then the devil brought him to Jerusalem, set him on the highest point of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,

note.term: the highest point of the temple

verse.note: The Greek word means a tip, edge or projecting part (literally 'little wing'), and it is not known which feature of the temple complex is meant. Suggestions include the roof edge of the sanctuary and a corner of the outer colonnades overlooking the Kidron valley. The traditional 'pinnacle' suggests a spire, which the temple did not have.

text.q: for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’
and: ‘On their hands they will lift you up, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone.’”

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “It has been said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
When the devil had finished every test, he withdrew from him until an opportune time.
Then Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and news about him went out through the whole surrounding region.
He was teaching in their synagogues and was praised by everyone.
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and as was his custom he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day and stood up to read.
The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, and unrolling the scroll he found the place where it was written:

text.q: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed out in release,

note.term: to bring good news to the poor
note.traditional: to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'to heal the brokenhearted' after 'he has sent me', which brings the quotation into line with Isaiah 61:1. The earliest witnesses lack the phrase, and it is generally regarded as a scribal addition. The quotation as Luke gives it combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6.

The same Greek noun appears twice in this verse and is rendered 'release' both times. It is the word Luke regularly uses for the forgiveness of sins. In the Greek Old Testament it is also the term for the release of debts and slaves in the Jubilee year. A first-century hearer could catch both associations, which English cannot convey with one word.

text.q: to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

verse.text: Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him.
And he began to say to them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
All spoke well of him and marveled at the words of grace that came from his mouth, and they were saying, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?”
verse.note: The phrase can mean that Jesus spoke winningly ('gracious words') or that he spoke about God's grace. Most translations choose the first, and the rendering here leaves both open. The crowd's reaction is also debated. Most take it as admiration that sours as Jesus goes on, but a minority reads the verbs as hostile from the start ('testified against him').

verse.text: He said to them, “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself! What we have heard happened in Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.’”
And he said, “Truly I tell you, no prophet finds favor in his hometown.
verse.note: The Greek adjective here is the same one used in verse 19 for the year 'of the Lord’s favor' (traditionally 'the acceptable year of the Lord'). It is rendered with 'favor' in both places so that the echo is audible. Jesus proclaims the year of God's favor and finds none in his own town.

text.q: But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land,

verse.note: The Greek word means both 'heaven' and 'sky'. Here it refers to the visible sky as the source of rain, and 'the sky was shut' is an idiom for drought. The story is told in 1 Kings 17–18.

text.q: yet Elijah was sent to none of them, but only to Zarephath in the territory of Sidon, to a widow there.

note.term: Zarephath in the territory of Sidon

verse.note: Zarephath was a Phoenician town outside Israel, and Naaman in the next verse was a commander in the army of Syria, Israel's enemy (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 5). Both of Jesus' examples are foreigners who received what Israelites did not. That explains the fury of the synagogue in verse 28.

text.q: And there were many people with skin disease in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, yet none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.”

verse.note: The traditional 'lepers' suggests modern leprosy (Hansen's disease). The Greek term, following the Hebrew of Leviticus 13–14, covered a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why the cure is called being 'cleansed'. It is widely agreed that the biblical term is broader than the modern disease, though many translations keep 'lepers' for familiarity.

verse.text: Everyone in the synagogue was filled with rage on hearing this.
They got up, drove him out of the town, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, intending to throw him off the cliff.
But he passed through the middle of them and went on his way.
He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbath.
They were astounded at his teaching, because his word had authority.
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice,

text.q: “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.”

verse.note: The Greek word may be an exclamation of surprise or displeasure, or the imperative of a verb meaning 'let be', which gives the older rendering 'Let us alone!'. Most recent scholarship takes it as an exclamation. The question that follows is an idiom, literally 'What to us and to you?', meaning roughly 'Why are you interfering with us?'

verse.text: Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” Then the demon threw the man down in their midst and came out of him without doing him any harm.
Amazement came over them all, and they kept saying to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
And talk of him was spreading to every place in the surrounding region.
He got up and left the synagogue and went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf.
Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her. At once she got up and began to serve them.
As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him, and laying his hands on each one of them, he healed them.
Demons also came out of many, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Messiah.
verse.note: The Greek word, traditionally 'Christ', is here a title with the article: the anointed king Israel was expecting. 'Messiah' is used where the title itself is the point, and 'Christ' where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: When day came, he went out and made his way to a deserted place. The crowds were searching for him, and they came to where he was and tried to keep him from leaving them.
But he said to them, “I must bring the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is what I was sent for.”
And he went on proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'Judea', while many later ones read 'Galilee', which fits the surrounding narrative and the parallel in Mark 1:39. 'Judea' is the harder reading and is probably original, with 'Galilee' a scribal correction. Luke sometimes uses 'Judea' broadly for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included, and that is likely the sense here.

verse.text: Once, while the crowd was pressing in on him and listening to the word of God, he was standing beside Lake Gennesaret,
verse.note: This is the body of water that Matthew, Mark and John call the Sea of Galilee. Luke consistently calls it a lake, the more exact term for an inland body of fresh water. Gennesaret was the name of the fertile plain on its north-western shore.

verse.text: and he saw two boats lying at the lake’s edge. The fishermen had got out of them and were washing their nets.
He got into one of the boats, the one that was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered, “Master, we worked hard all night and caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the nets.”
When they had done this, they enclosed a great number of fish, and their nets were beginning to tear.
So they signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came, and they filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at the knees of Jesus and said, “Go away from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord!”
For amazement had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish they had taken,
and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were in partnership with Simon. Then Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
verse.note: Most translations have simply ‘catch’, echoing ‘fishers of people’ in Matthew and Mark. Luke’s verb is not a fishing term: it means to capture alive, and in the Septuagint it is used of sparing the lives of captives in war. ‘Alive’ is kept here because that is the element the verb specifies. Its only other New Testament use is 2 Timothy 2:26.

verse.text: And when they had brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
While he was in one of the towns, there was a man covered with a skin disease. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”
verse.note: The Greek word, like the Hebrew term it translates in Leviticus 13–14, covered a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean. It is not the specific illness now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease), and may not have included it. Most translations keep ‘leprosy’ and explain this in a footnote. The man asks to be made ‘clean’ rather than healed because the condition barred him from normal community and worship.

verse.text: He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing. Be made clean.” And at once the skin disease left him.
And he ordered him to tell no one: “Instead, go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing as Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: Leviticus 14 requires a person whose skin disease has cleared to be examined by a priest and to bring prescribed offerings before returning to ordinary life. ‘A testimony to them’ may mean proof to the priests or to people generally that the man is clean; the Greek does not specify.

verse.text: But the news about him spread all the more, and large crowds were gathering to listen and to be healed of their illnesses.
But he himself would withdraw to deserted places and pray.

One day, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and the power of the Lord was present for him to heal.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read ‘to heal them’, and the King James tradition follows that reading. The earliest witnesses have ‘him’ as the one doing the healing, which is the reading translated here. ‘The Lord’ in this phrase refers to God, whose power is at work in Jesus.

verse.text: Just then some men came carrying on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him in front of Jesus.
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him, stretcher and all, through the tiles into the middle, in front of Jesus.
When he saw their faith, he said, “Friend, your sins have been forgiven you.”
The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
But Jesus, aware of their reasoning, answered them, “Why are you reasoning this way in your hearts?

text.q: Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins have been forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” he said to the paralysed man, “I say to you, get up, pick up your stretcher, and go to your house.”
At once he stood up in front of them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went off to his house, glorifying God.
Astonishment seized them all, and they glorified God. They were filled with fear and said, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
After this he went out and noticed a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.”
verse.note: These men collected tolls and customs duties on goods, usually working for contractors who had bought the right to collect them. Some scholars prefer ‘toll collector’ for that reason. They were widely regarded as dishonest and as collaborators with Rome or its client rulers, which is why they are paired with ‘sinners’ in verse 30.

verse.text: And he left everything behind, got up, and began to follow him.
Then Levi gave a great banquet for him in his house, and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining at table with them.
The Pharisees and their scribes were grumbling to his disciples, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.

text.q: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to turning back.”

verse.note: ‘Repentance’ now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: They said to him, “John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.”
He said to them, “Can you make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?
verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘the sons of the bridal chamber’, a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or the bridegroom’s attendants in particular, and translations vary between the two. Fasting during a wedding celebration would have been unthinkable.

text.q: But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days.”

verse.text: He also told them a parable: “No one tears a patch from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Otherwise, he will tear the new, and the patch from the new will not match the old.

text.q: And no one puts young wine into old wineskins. Otherwise, the young wine will burst the skins; it will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined.

verse.note: Most translations have ‘new wine’ and ‘fresh’ or ‘new’ wineskins. The Greek uses two different adjectives: one meaning recent or young for the wine, and another meaning new or unused for the garment and the wineskins. ‘Young’ and ‘new’ keep the two apart. Wine that is still fermenting would split old skins that had lost their stretch.

text.q: No, young wine must be put into new wineskins.
And no one who has drunk old wine wants young, for they say, ‘The old is good.’”

verse.note: This verse is absent from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts, though most scholars consider it original to Luke. Many later manuscripts read ‘better’ in place of ‘good’; the earliest witnesses have ‘good’. The saying is usually taken as a wry comment on those who are content with the old and will not try the new.

verse.text: One Sabbath he happened to be passing through grainfields, and his disciples were picking the heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands, and eating them.

note.traditional: on the second sabbath after the first

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “on the second-first Sabbath”, using a word found nowhere else whose meaning is unknown. The earliest witnesses lack it, and the SBLGNT, like most modern editions, omits it.

Picking grain by hand while walking through someone else’s field was allowed by the Law (Deuteronomy 23:25), so the complaint is not about theft. The objection is that picking and rubbing out the kernels counted as reaping and threshing, and so as work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verse.text: But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath?”
Jesus answered them, “Have you not even read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him:

text.q: how he went into the house of God, took the loaves of presentation and ate them, and gave some to those with him, though no one is permitted to eat them except the priests alone?”

note.traditional: the bread of the Presence / the showbread

verse.note: “Bread of the Presence” translates the Hebrew name; the Greek phrase, taken from the Septuagint, means the loaves “of the setting out”, that is, loaves presented before God. Twelve loaves were laid out in the sanctuary each Sabbath, and the old ones were eaten only by priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). The story of David is in 1 Samuel 21.

verse.text: And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.”
On another Sabbath he went into the synagogue and taught. A man was there whose right hand was withered.
The scribes and the Pharisees were watching him closely to see whether he would cure on the Sabbath, so that they might find a charge to bring against him.
But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.” And he got up and stood there.
Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you: is it permitted on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to destroy it?”
And looking around at them all, he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and his hand was restored.
But they were filled with senseless fury and began discussing with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word means a lack of sense or understanding. Most translators take it here as irrational rage; a minority read it as bewilderment, with the opponents at a loss what to do. The rendering keeps both the folly and the anger in view.

verse.text: In those days he went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the whole night in prayer to God.
And when day came, he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles:
Simon, whom he also named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip and Bartholomew,
and Matthew and Thomas, and James son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot,
verse.note: The word means a zealous person, an enthusiast, and was used for those fiercely devoted to the Law. Whether it links Simon to the armed revolutionary party called Zealots during the war of 66–70 is disputed, since that party is not clearly attested as an organised group this early. Matthew and Mark give the Aramaic equivalent, “Cananaean”.

verse.text: and Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verse.note: The Greek says only “Judas of James”. That construction normally names a father, and most modern translations render it “son of James”. Older versions wrote “brother of James”, identifying him with the author of the letter of Jude.

verse.text: And coming down with them, he stood on a level place, along with a large crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of the people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon,
who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. Those troubled by unclean spirits were being cured,
and the whole crowd was trying to touch him, because power was going out from him and healing them all.
Then he raised his eyes to his disciples and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

text.q: Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will eat your fill. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they shut you out and insult you and throw out your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice on that day and leap for joy, for look, your reward is great in heaven; for their ancestors treated the prophets in just the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, for you have been paid your comfort in full.

note.term: you have been paid your comfort in full

verse.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts from the period for “paid in full”, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone: the account is settled and nothing more is owed. Modern translations commonly say “have received” or “have received in full”.

text.q: Woe to you who are full now, for you will go hungry. Woe, you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.
Woe when all people speak well of you, for their ancestors treated the false prophets in just the same way.
But to you who are listening I say: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.
To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other as well; and from the one who takes your cloak, do not hold back your tunic either.
Give to everyone who asks you, and from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back.
And just as you want people to do to you, do the same to them.
If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.

note.term: what credit is that to you
note.traditional: what thank have ye / what credit is that to you

verse.note: The word is the one usually translated “grace” or “favour”. Here it may mean the thanks or credit such conduct earns, as most translations take it, or the favour it finds with God. Matthew’s parallel has “reward”.

text.q: And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same.
And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, so as to get back the same amount.
Rather, love your enemies and do good and lend, expecting nothing back. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he himself is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

note.traditional: hoping for nothing again / expecting nothing in return

verse.note: Elsewhere in Greek this verb means “to despair”, which would give “despairing of nothing”, or, with a variant found in some manuscripts, “despairing of no one”. The contrast with verse 34, lending in the hope of receiving, favours “expecting nothing back”. Most translators adopt that sense, though it is not otherwise attested this early.

text.q: Be compassionate, just as your Father is compassionate.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “merciful”. This word is a different one from the usual New Testament term for mercy; it refers to pity felt for someone in distress, and in the Septuagint it describes God as compassionate (as in Exodus 34:6). “Compassionate” keeps the two words distinct.

text.q: And do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Pardon, and you will be pardoned;

note.term: Pardon, and you will be pardoned
note.traditional: forgive, and you will be forgiven

verse.note: The verb is not the usual word for forgiving. It means to release or let go, and it was used of freeing a prisoner, acquitting a defendant or cancelling a debt. After “judge” and “condemn” the courtroom sense fits, so “pardon” is used; most translations have “forgive”.

text.q: give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be given into your lap; for with the measure you measure out, it will be measured back to you.”

note.term: will be given into your lap

verse.note: The picture is of a grain seller filling a measure generously and pouring it into the fold of the buyer’s outer garment, which was pulled up over the belt to form a pouch. The Greek says “they will give”, an indefinite plural that probably refers to God’s action.

verse.text: He also told them a parable: “Can a blind person guide a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?

text.q: A disciple is not above the teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher.
Why do you look at the splinter in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?

How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the splinter that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the splinter that is in your brother’s eye.
For there is no good tree that bears bad fruit, nor again a bad tree that bears good fruit.
For each tree is known by its own fruit. People do not gather figs from thornbushes, nor do they pick grapes from a bramble.

The good person, out of the good treasure of his heart, brings out what is good, and the evil person, out of the evil treasure, brings out what is evil; for his mouth speaks out of the overflow of the heart.
Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what that person is like:

that person is like someone building a house, who dug and went down deep and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood came, the river burst against that house and was not strong enough to shake it, because it had been well built.

note.term: because it had been well built
note.traditional: for it was founded upon a rock

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “for it had been founded on the rock”, which matches Matthew 7:25. The earliest witnesses have “because it had been well built”, and the other reading is generally regarded as a harmonisation to Matthew.

text.q: But the one who has heard and has not done them is like someone who built a house on the ground without a foundation. The river burst against it, and at once it collapsed, and the ruin of that house was great.”

verse.text: When he had finished saying all this in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum.
A certain centurion had a slave whom he valued highly, and this slave was sick and about to die.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee. ‘Servant’ became the usual English rendering when that word could cover both; today it suggests paid domestic work. Many modern translations and most scholars now use ‘slave’.

verse.text: When he heard about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his slave’s life.
When they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you grant him this,

text.q: for he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.”

verse.note: This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated ‘Gentiles’. In the singular it means a people or nation, and here the Jewish elders use it of their own people.

verse.text: So Jesus went with them. He was already not far from the house when the centurion sent friends to say to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not fit to have you come under my roof.
verse.note: The Greek form of address ranges from a polite ‘Sir’ to ‘Lord’ in the full religious sense. ‘Lord’ is the usual rendering here and fits the centurion’s marked deference, but the word alone does not show how much he meant by it.

text.q: That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to you either. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.

verse.note: The centurion’s message uses a different word here from the ‘slave’ of verses 2, 3, 8 and 10. It can mean ‘child’, ‘boy’ or ‘servant’. Since Luke identifies the person as the centurion’s slave, ‘servant’ is chosen. Some hear a note of affection in the word, though that is not certain.

text.q: For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

verse.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed at him. Turning to the crowd that was following him, he said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”
And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the slave in good health.
Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a large crowd went along with him.
As he approached the town gate, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A considerable crowd from the town was with her.
When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her, “Do not weep.”
Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I say to you, rise!”
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verse.note: The wording matches the Greek version of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah restores a widow’s son to life and gives him back to his mother. The crowd’s acclamation of ‘a great prophet’ in the next verse fits that echo.

verse.text: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has risen among us!” and, “God has come to help his people!”
verse.note: In the Greek Scriptures this verb is used of God turning his attention to his people to rescue or care for them, a sense the modern English ‘visit’ no longer conveys. Most translations keep ‘visited’; a few render it along the lines chosen here.

verse.text: This report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding region.
John’s disciples reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him,
sent them to the Lord to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”
When the men came to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you to ask, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”
At that very time he healed many people of diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and he granted sight to many who were blind.

And he answered them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, those with skin disease are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news proclaimed to them.
verse.note: The list echoes Isaiah’s descriptions of the time of God’s deliverance (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). Jesus answers John’s question not by claiming a title but by pointing to events that Scripture associated with that time.

The Greek term, following Leviticus 13–14, covers a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean. It is not the same as modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease) and may not include it. That is why such people are said to be ‘cleansed’ and not simply healed. Most translations keep ‘lepers’, often with a footnote to this effect.

text.q: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

note.term: does not stumble because of me
note.traditional: is not offended in me / takes no offense at me

verse.note: The verb means to be tripped up or made to fall. Here it means being put off from trusting Jesus because he does not match expectations, which is stronger than the modern sense of taking offense. Several modern translations also use ‘stumble’.

verse.text: When John’s messengers had left, he began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

text.q: What, then, did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear splendid clothes and live in luxury are in royal palaces.
What, then, did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way ahead of you.’

verse.note: The quotation combines Malachi 3:1 with wording from Exodus 23:20. The Greek word for ‘messenger’ is the one usually translated ‘angel’; it is also used of John’s own messengers in verse 24.

text.q: I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

verse.text: (All the people who heard, even the tax collectors, vindicated God, having been baptized with John’s baptism;
verse.note: The verb belongs to a single Greek word-family that English splits between ‘righteous/just’ and ‘justify’. Here it means to acknowledge or show that God is in the right, and it recurs in verse 35 of wisdom. Other translations paraphrase, for example ‘acknowledged the justice of God’ or ‘declared God just’.

Verses 29–30 are taken here as Luke’s own aside, following the punctuation of the Greek edition and many modern translations. They can also be read as a continuation of Jesus’s speech. The Greek does not say what was heard: on the first reading it is probably Jesus’s words about John, on the second John’s preaching.

verse.text: but the Pharisees and the experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verse.note: The term refers to specialists in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, not to courtroom advocates as ‘lawyers’ now suggests. Several modern translations render it as here.

text.q: “To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation? What are they like?
They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, who say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not weep.’
For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
Yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

verse.text: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table.

note.traditional: sat down to eat / took his place at the table

verse.note: At formal meals guests lay on couches, propped on one elbow, with their feet stretched out away from the table. This is how the woman can stand behind Jesus and yet be at his feet in verse 38.

verse.text: Now there was a woman in the town who was a sinner. When she learned that he was reclining at the table in the Pharisee’s house, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume
and stood behind him at his feet, weeping. She began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet again and again, and anointed them with the perfume.
When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what kind of woman this is who is touching him, that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He said, “Say it, Teacher.”

text.q: “Two people were in debt to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer (compare Matthew 20:2). The two debts are thus about five hundred and fifty days’ pay.

text.q: Since they could not repay, he canceled the debts of both. So which of them will love him more?”

verse.text: Simon answered, “I suppose the one for whom he canceled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.”

Then, turning toward the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I came into your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.

text.q: You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not stopped kissing my feet.
You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.
For this reason, I tell you, her sins, many as they are, have been forgiven, for she loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little.”

verse.note: The Greek can be read as giving the cause of her forgiveness (she is forgiven because she loved) or the evidence for it (her love shows that she has been forgiven). The parable, in which love follows the canceling of the debt, and the second half of the verse favor the second reading, which most interpreters adopt. ‘For’ leaves both open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: Then he said to her, “Your sins have been forgiven.”
Those reclining at the table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”
But he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Soon afterward he went traveling through town and village, proclaiming and announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him,
and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses: Mary, the one called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, and Susanna, and many others, who were providing for them out of their own means.
verse.note: The Herod meant here is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great and ruler of Galilee during Jesus’ ministry. The Greek word covers a manager of a household or estate; Chuza’s exact office is not known, but Joanna evidently belonged to court circles and had money of her own.

verse.text: As a large crowd was gathering and people from town after town were making their way to him, he spoke by means of a parable:

text.q: “The sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it up.

verse.note: The Greek word is the one usually translated ‘heaven’, here in its ordinary sense of the visible sky. The traditional ‘birds of the air’ is an English idiom; ‘sky’ is what the word means in this phrase.

text.q: Other seed fell on the rock, and when it sprouted it withered, because it had no moisture.
Other seed fell in the middle of the thorns, and the thorns sprouted along with it and choked it.

verse.text: And other seed fell into the good soil, and when it sprouted it produced fruit a hundredfold.” As he said these things he called out, “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear!”
His disciples asked him what this parable meant.
He said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but to the rest it comes in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

note.term: so that seeing they may not see
note.traditional: that seeing they might not see

verse.note: The words echo Isaiah 6:9–10, where the prophet is sent to a people who will hear without understanding. The Greek conjunction normally expresses purpose, and it is translated that way here. Some interpreters take it as expressing result, or as shorthand for ‘so that the scripture is fulfilled’; the parallel in Matthew 13:13 has ‘because’.

text.q: Now this is what the parable means: the seed is the word of God.
Those along the path are the ones who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a time, and in a time of testing they fall away.

verse.note: The older English tradition has ‘temptation’, which now suggests enticement to sin. In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, the word covers any trial that puts loyalty to the proof, and the parallel accounts speak of trouble and persecution. Many modern versions also have ‘testing’ here.

text.q: As for what fell into the thorns, these are the ones who have heard, but as they go on their way they are choked by the worries and wealth and pleasures of life, and they bring no fruit to maturity.
But as for what is in the fine soil, these are the ones who, having heard the word with a fine and good heart, hold on to it and bear fruit with endurance.

verse.note: Luke pairs two Greek words for ‘good’ that together formed a stock phrase in Greek for a person of sound and admirable character. The first is the same word used of the soil earlier in the verse, so ‘fine’ is used for both to keep the link. The parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark do not have the phrase.

text.q: No one lights a lamp and then covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he puts it on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
For nothing is hidden that will not be brought into the open, and nothing concealed that will not be known and come into the open.
So take care how you listen. For to whoever has, more will be given; and from whoever does not have, even what they think they have will be taken away.”

verse.text: His mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd.
He was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wanting to see you.”
But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these: the ones who hear the word of God and do it.”
One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake.” So they put out.
As they sailed he fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and they were being swamped and were in danger.
They came and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” He woke and rebuked the wind and the surging water; they stopped, and there was a calm.
He said to them, “Where is your faith?” Afraid and amazed, they said to one another, “Who then is this, that he gives orders even to the winds and the water, and they obey him?”
They came to land in the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided here and in verse 37 between Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes, and the same variation occurs in the parallel accounts. Gerasa was a city more than thirty miles from the lake and Gadara a few miles from it, which probably prompted the changes. SBLGNT reads Gerasenes; the older English tradition has Gadarenes.

verse.text: As he stepped out onto the land, a man from the town who had demons met him. For a long time he had worn no clothing, and he did not live in a house but among the tombs.
When he saw Jesus, he cried out, fell down before him, and said in a loud voice, “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me!”

For Jesus had been commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him; he would be bound with chains and shackles and kept under guard, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the deserted places.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean either ‘on many occasions’ or ‘for a long time’. The first is chosen because the sentence goes on to describe repeated binding and escape, but the second is equally possible grammatically.

verse.text: Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,” because many demons had entered him.
verse.note: A Latin military term taken into Greek. A Roman legion at full strength numbered roughly five to six thousand soldiers, so the name signals a vast number and would have carried overtones of an occupying force.

verse.text: And they kept pleading with him not to order them to go away into the abyss.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament the word is used for the primeval deep. In Jewish writing of the period it had also come to mean a place where rebellious spirits are confined, a sense also found in Revelation. The parallel in Mark 5:10 has the demons ask not to be sent out of the region.

verse.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they pleaded with him to permit them to enter those. He permitted them.
The demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the town and in the countryside.
People went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it told them how the man who had been possessed by demons was saved.
verse.note: Most translations have ‘healed’ here and ‘made you well’ in verses 48 and 50, but ‘saved’ in verse 12. Luke uses one verb throughout, which covered rescue from danger, disease and death as well as salvation in the religious sense. Verse 48 also repeats word for word what Jesus says to the forgiven woman in 7:50. One English word is kept so the reader can see the connection Luke’s first readers would have heard.

verse.text: Then the whole population of the surrounding region of the Gerasenes asked him to go away from them, because they were gripped by great fear. So he got into a boat and returned.
The man from whom the demons had gone out begged to be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying,
“Return to your home, and recount all that God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole town all that Jesus had done for him.
