When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all expecting him.
Just then a man named Jairus came, a leader of the synagogue. Falling at the feet of Jesus, he pleaded with him to come to his house,
because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the crowds were smothering him.
And a woman who had had a flow of blood for twelve years, and who, though she had spent her whole livelihood on physicians, could not be healed by anyone,

note.term: though she had spent her whole livelihood on physicians
note.traditional: which had spent all her living upon physicians

verse.note: These words are missing from some early and important manuscripts, and some editions bracket them and some translations omit them. SBLGNT prints them as part of the text. A similar statement stands without dispute in Mark 5:26.

verse.text: came up behind him and touched the tassel of his cloak, and at once her flow of blood stopped.
verse.note: Traditional renderings are ‘hem’, ‘border’, ‘fringe’ or ‘edge’, and the word can mean simply the edge of a garment. In the Greek Old Testament it is the term for the tassels Israelite men were commanded to wear on the corners of their garments (Numbers 15:38–39). That is probably what a first-century reader would picture on a Jewish teacher’s cloak, though the plainer sense cannot be ruled out.

verse.text: Jesus said, “Who is it that touched me?” When everyone denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds are hemming you in and pressing against you.”
But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I knew that power had gone out from me.”
When the woman saw that she had not escaped notice, she came trembling, fell down before him, and told before all the people why she had touched him and how she had been cured at once.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
While he was still speaking, someone came from the synagogue leader’s house and said, “Your daughter has died. Do not trouble the teacher any longer.”
But Jesus heard this and answered him, “Do not be afraid. Only believe, and she will be saved.”
When he came to the house, he did not allow anyone to go in with him except Peter, John, and James, and the child’s father and mother.
Everyone was weeping and mourning for her. But he said, “Do not weep, for she has not died but is sleeping.”
And they laughed at him, knowing that she had died.
But he took hold of her hand and called out, “Child, get up!”
Her spirit came back, and she stood up at once, and he directed that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were astounded, but he commanded them to tell no one what had happened.
Calling the Twelve together, he gave them power and authority over all the demons and to heal diseases,
and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to cure the sick.
He said to them, “Take nothing for the journey: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, and do not have two tunics apiece.

text.q: Whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there.
And wherever people do not welcome you, as you leave that town shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them.”

verse.text: So they set out and went from village to village, bringing the good news and healing everywhere.
Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was thoroughly perplexed, because it was being said by some that John had been raised from the dead,
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. A tetrarch was a dependent prince ranking below a king. Luke 3:19–20 has already reported that he imprisoned John the Baptist; John's execution is mentioned in Luke only here, in Herod's own words.

verse.text: by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the ancient prophets had risen.
But Herod said, “John I beheaded. Who then is this, about whom I hear such things?” And he kept trying to see him.
When the apostles returned, they told him all that they had done. Then he took them along and withdrew privately to a town called Bethsaida.
But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and he cured those who needed healing.

The day began to decline, and the Twelve came to him and said, “Send the crowd away so that they can go to the surrounding villages and farms to find lodging and provisions, for we are in a deserted place here.”
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we ourselves go and buy food for all these people.”
For there were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples, “Have them recline in groups of about fifty.”
verse.note: Most English versions say 'sit down'. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for taking one's place at a meal, which was done reclining, and only Luke uses it in the New Testament. Keeping 'recline' lets the scene read as a hosted meal and not merely a seated crowd.

verse.text: They did so and had them all recline.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
They all ate and were filled, and what they had left over was collected: twelve baskets of broken pieces.
Once, when he was praying in private and the disciples were with him, he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?”
They answered, “John the Baptist; but others say Elijah, and others that one of the ancient prophets has risen.”
He said to them, “But you—who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “The Messiah of God.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'the Christ of God'. Here the word is a title, God's anointed king whom Israel expected, and not a name, so 'Messiah' conveys what Peter's hearers would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

verse.text: But he gave them a stern warning and ordered them to tell this to no one,
saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”
Then he said to everyone, “If anyone wants to come after me, they must deny themselves and take up their cross every day and follow me.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake, that person will save it.

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a person's physical life and the person's self; older versions sometimes render it 'soul' in the parallel passages. The saying plays on that range: clinging to one's life loses the self that matters. Verse 25 makes this explicit by replacing the word with 'themselves'.

text.q: For what good does it do a person to gain the whole world and yet lose or forfeit themselves?
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
But I tell you truly, there are some of those standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: About eight days after these words, he took Peter and John and James along and went up the mountain to pray.
And as he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing became white, flashing like lightning.
And look, two men were talking with him; they were Moses and Elijah,
who appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to fulfill in Jerusalem.
verse.note: The Greek word is exodos. It was an ordinary euphemism for death, but it is also the Septuagint's word for Israel's going out from Egypt. With Moses standing in the scene, most interpreters think Luke intends both senses: Jesus' death, resurrection and ascension as a new act of deliverance.

verse.text: Now Peter and those with him had been weighed down with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men standing with him.
verse.note: The verb is rare and can mean either 'wake up fully' or 'stay awake throughout'. On the second reading the disciples fought off sleep and saw the whole event: 'but since they had stayed awake'. Translations are divided, and the context does not settle it.

verse.text: As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three shelters, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.” He did not know what he was saying.
verse.note: Older versions have 'tabernacles' and many modern ones 'tents'. The word means a tent or temporary hut, and on a mountainside a shelter of branches is more likely than a tent. Many interpreters see an allusion to the Feast of Booths, when such huts were built, though that is not certain.

verse.text: While he was saying this, a cloud came and began to overshadow them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.
And a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, the Chosen One. Listen to him!”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'my Son, the Chosen One', which echoes Isaiah 42:1. Most later manuscripts read 'my beloved Son', probably assimilated to the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark and to the voice at Jesus' baptism. Critical editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading.

verse.text: When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent, and in those days they told no one anything of what they had seen.
On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.
And look, a man from the crowd shouted, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, because he is my only child,

text.q: and look, a spirit seizes him, and suddenly he screams; it convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and it will hardly leave him, and it is crushing him.
I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they could not.”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “You unbelieving and twisted generation, how long shall I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'perverse', which now tends to suggest sexual deviance. The Greek word means bent out of shape or turned from the right way. The phrase echoes the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5, where Moses calls Israel a crooked and twisted generation.

verse.text: While the boy was still approaching, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him violently. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, cured the boy, and gave him back to his father.
And all were astounded at the majesty of God. While everyone was marveling at all that he was doing, he said to his disciples,

text.q: “Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands.”

verse.text: But they did not understand this saying. It was veiled from them so that they would not grasp it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
Then a thought came up among them: which of them might be the greatest?

note.term: a thought came up among them

verse.note: The Greek word can mean an inward reasoning or an open dispute, and the phrase can be read 'among them' or 'within them'. Most translations have 'an argument arose', in line with Mark 9:34. Since Luke at once says Jesus knew 'the thought of their hearts', using the same word, it is rendered 'thought' in both verses, but an open argument remains possible.

verse.text: But Jesus, knowing the thought of their hearts, took a little child and had the child stand beside him,
and said to them, “Whoever welcomes this little child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. For the one who is least among all of you, that one is great.”
John spoke up and said, “Master, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow along with us.”
But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you.”
As the days were being fulfilled for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem,

note.term: for him to be taken up
note.traditional: that he should be received up

verse.note: The noun occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb is used of Jesus' ascension in Acts 1, and most scholars take it here as the ascension, perhaps including the death and resurrection that lead to it. A minority take it simply as a term for his death.

verse.text: and he sent messengers before his face. They went and entered a Samaritan village to make things ready for him,
but the people there did not welcome him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

note.term: because his face was set toward Jerusalem
note.traditional: because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem

verse.note: Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim and rejected the Jerusalem temple, and relations between the two communities were hostile. Pilgrims crossing Samaria on their way to Jerusalem could not count on hospitality. The village's refusal is about the destination, not about Jesus personally.

verse.text: When the disciples James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?”
But he turned and rebuked them.

note.term: But he turned and rebuked them.
note.traditional: But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add words of Jesus at the end of verse 55 and the start of verse 56: 'You do not know what kind of spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them.' Some also add 'as Elijah did' to verse 54, making explicit the allusion to 2 Kings 1. The earliest manuscripts lack these words, and critical editions omit them as later additions.

verse.text: And they went on to another village.
As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.”
Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”
But he said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God everywhere.”
Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord; but first let me say goodbye to those at my home.”
But Jesus said, “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him two by two into every town and place where he himself was about to go.
verse.note: The manuscripts are closely divided between "seventy-two" and "seventy," here and in verse 17, and scholars do not agree which is original. The SBLGNT reads seventy-two. Either number may echo the traditional count of the world's nations in Genesis 10, which differs in the same way between the Hebrew and Greek texts.

verse.text: He said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.

text.q: Go! Look, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’
And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you.

verse.note: "Son of" followed by a quality is a Semitic idiom for a person characterised by that quality. Here it means someone who is disposed to peace and ready to receive the messengers' greeting. Many modern translations paraphrase as "a person of peace" or "someone who promotes peace."

text.q: Stay in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not move around from house to house.
And whatever town you enter where they welcome you, eat what is set before you,
heal the sick who are there, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
But whatever town you enter where they do not welcome you, go out into its streets and say,
‘Even the dust from your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.’
I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is "repented," which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English "repent" centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of that turning.

text.q: But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.
Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.”

verse.text: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name!”
He said to them, “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

text.q: Look, I have given you the authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you at all.
Yet do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in the heavens.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural here, unlike the singular in verses 15, 18 and 21. Most translations flatten it to "heaven." The plural reflects a Semitic way of speaking about God's dwelling and is kept where the Greek has it. The image is of a heavenly register of citizens.

verse.text: At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was your good pleasure.
verse.note: Many translations have "I thank you." In the Greek Psalms this verb regularly renders the Hebrew for openly acknowledging and praising God, which is broader than gratitude. Some modern versions also use "praise."

text.q: Everything has been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

verse.text: Then, turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.

text.q: For I tell you that many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

verse.text: Just then an expert in the law stood up to test him, saying, “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is "lawyer," which now suggests a courtroom advocate. The man is a specialist in interpreting the Law of Moses, a religious scholar. Several modern translations render it in a similar way.

The adjective is formed from the word for "age." In Jewish usage of the period "eternal life" is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. "Eternal" is the standard rendering and is kept here. A minority of translators prefer "life of the age to come."

verse.text: He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.’”
He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this and you will live.”
But he, wanting to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English divides between "righteous/righteousness" and "just/justice/justify." The verb here means to show oneself to be in the right. The man wants to come out of the exchange vindicated, perhaps for having asked a question whose answer he already knew.

verse.text: Jesus took up the question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among bandits, who stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes violent brigands who operate in gangs, not sneak thieves. "Robbers" is the usual modern rendering and is not wrong. "Bandits" better conveys the armed highwaymen for whom the steep, desolate road from Jerusalem down to Jericho was known.

text.q: By chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a Samaritan who was on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion.

verse.note: Samaritans and Jews both revered the Law of Moses but worshipped at rival sanctuaries, and they regarded each other with long-standing hostility. In the previous chapter a Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus. The original hearers would have expected the third traveller, after a priest and a Levite, to be an ordinary Israelite, not a despised outsider.

text.q: He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. Two would probably have covered a stay of some days at an inn, though exact costs are uncertain.

text.q: Which of these three, do you think, became a neighbor to the man who fell among the bandits?”

verse.text: He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go, and you do the same.”
As they went on their way, he entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him.
She had a sister called Mary, who sat down at the feet of Jesus and was listening to his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving. She came up and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.”
The Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,

text.q: but few things are needed, or only one. For Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

note.term: few things are needed, or only one

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. Many read simply "but one thing is needed," which most translations follow. Others, including some early witnesses, read "few things are needed, or one," and this is the reading the SBLGNT prints. On the longer reading Jesus may be moving from the meal (a few dishes would do, or even one) to the one thing that matters, which Mary has chosen.

verse.text: Now he was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, may your name be held holy. May your kingdom come.

note.traditional: Our Father who art in heaven

verse.note: Luke's form of the prayer is shorter than Matthew's. Many later manuscripts expand it toward the Matthean wording ('Our Father in the heavens', 'your will be done', 'rescue us from the evil one'), but the earliest witnesses lack these lines, and the short form is translated here.

note.term: may your name be held holy

verse.note: 'Hallowed' is the traditional word and means exactly this, but it is no longer in ordinary use. The verb asks that God's name be treated as holy; the passive probably implies that God himself is asked to bring this about.

text.q: Give us each day our daily bread.

verse.note: The Greek word is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer, and its meaning is genuinely uncertain. The main proposals are 'for the coming day', 'necessary for existence' and 'for today'. The traditional 'daily' is kept because no alternative is secure.

text.q: And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not bring us into testing.’”

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a trial that tests faithfulness and an enticement to sin; in the Septuagint and in this period the first sense is the more usual. Most translations keep 'temptation', and some give 'time of trial'. The same word family appears in verse 16, where people 'test' Jesus.

verse.text: And he said to them, “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves,

text.q: because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
and he will answer from inside, ‘Do not bother me. The door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’?
I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will rise and give him as much as he needs.

verse.note: In Greek usage of the period the word means lack of shame, impudence; evidence that it meant 'persistence' is weak, though many translations render it so in light of the parable's use. It is usually taken as the nerve of the man who knocks at midnight. Some scholars refer it instead to the man in bed, who acts to avoid being shamed for refusing a neighbour.

text.q: And I tell you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
Which father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will hand him a snake instead of a fish?
Or if he asks for an egg, will hand him a scorpion?
If you then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

verse.text: He was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds were amazed.
But some of them said, “He casts out the demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.”
Others, to test him, were seeking from him a sign from heaven.
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house.

text.q: And if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out the demons by Beelzebul.
But if I cast out the demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

verse.note: The phrase echoes Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's magicians, unable to match a plague, admit, 'This is the finger of God.' It means God's own direct power at work. The parallel in Matthew 12:28 has 'the Spirit of God'.

text.q: When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his possessions are safe.
But when someone stronger than he attacks and overcomes him, he takes away the armor on which he relied and divides up his spoils.
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
When the unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house that I came out of.’
And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order.
Then it goes and brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and settle there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

verse.text: As he was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that carried you, and the breasts that nursed you!”
But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!”
verse.note: The Greek particle can correct ('No, rather'), or affirm and go further ('Yes, but even more'). The rendering leaves this open as far as English allows. Most interpreters think Jesus does not deny the woman's words but redirects them to what matters more.

verse.text: As the crowds were growing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.

text.q: For just as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so also the Son of Man will be to this generation.

The queen of the South will be raised at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look, something greater than Solomon is here.
The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they turned back at the proclamation of Jonah, and look, something greater than Jonah is here.

verse.note: 'Repent' in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word here carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which is what the people of Nineveh did in the book of Jonah. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on the lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
The lamp of the body is your eye. When your eye is generous, your whole body also is full of light; but when it is stingy, your body also is dark.

verse.note: The word literally means 'single' or 'sound', and most translations render it 'healthy', keeping the physical picture of the eye. In Jewish idiom a 'good eye' is generosity and an 'evil eye' is grudging stinginess; 'stingy' here renders the ordinary Greek word for 'evil'. This translation follows the idiom, at the cost of the physical image, and the mainstream rendering remains defensible, particularly in Luke, where the surrounding context is about light rather than money.

text.q: See to it, then, that the light in you is not darkness.
If then your whole body is full of light, with no part of it dark, it will be wholly full of light, as when the lamp illuminates you with its brightness.”

verse.text: When he had spoken, a Pharisee asked him to have a meal at his house; so he went in and reclined at table.
The Pharisee was amazed when he saw that he did not first wash before the meal.
verse.note: The verb is the one usually rendered 'baptize'. Here it refers to a ritual washing before eating, a matter of purity rather than hygiene, which Pharisaic tradition required though the Law of Moses did not command it of ordinary people at ordinary meals.

verse.text: But the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.

text.q: Fools! Did not the one who made the outside make the inside also?
But give what is inside as alms, and look, everything is clean for you.

note.term: give what is inside as alms

verse.note: The Greek is compressed. It is taken here to mean giving away the contents of the cup and dish to the poor. Others understand 'as for what is inside, give alms', or 'give alms from within', that is, from the heart. 'Alms' are charitable gifts to those in need.

text.q: But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every garden herb, and pass over justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the front seat in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked tombs, and the people who walk over them do not know it.”

verse.note: Under the Law, contact with a grave made a person ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so graves were marked to warn passers-by. Anyone walking over an unmarked one became unclean without knowing it. The charge is that the Pharisees, who were devoted to purity, were themselves a hidden source of defilement.

verse.text: One of the experts in the law answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us too.”
verse.note: 'Lawyer' now suggests an attorney who represents clients in court. These were specialists in interpreting the Law of Moses and its application to daily life. Several modern translations already use 'experts in the law'.

verse.text: He said, “Woe to you experts in the law as well! For you load people with burdens hard to carry, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

text.q: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and it was your ancestors who killed them.
So you are witnesses, and you approve of the deeds of your ancestors, because they killed them and you build.
For this reason also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute,’

verse.note: No known passage of Scripture contains these words. The phrase may personify God's wisdom as a speaker, as Proverbs does, or it may refer to a writing now lost, or to God's wise decree; in Matthew 23:34 the saying is given in Jesus' own voice. Where the quotation ends is also uncertain; it is closed here at the end of verse 49.

text.q: so that this generation may be held accountable for the blood of all the prophets shed since the foundation of the world,
from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, this generation will be held accountable for it.

note.term: from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah

verse.note: Abel is the first person murdered in Genesis. Zechariah is usually identified with the priest stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; in the arrangement of the Hebrew Scriptures that places Chronicles last, the pair spans the first and last murders in Scripture. 'The sanctuary' renders the Greek 'the house', meaning the temple building.

text.q: Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not go in yourselves, and you hindered those who were going in.”

verse.text: When he went out from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to oppose him fiercely and to interrogate him about many things,
lying in wait for him, to catch him in something out of his own mouth.

Meanwhile, when the crowd had gathered in its thousands, so that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first: “Be on your guard against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
verse.note: The Greek adverb can attach to what precedes (he addressed his disciples first, before turning to the crowd) or to what follows (“First of all, be on your guard”). Most modern translations take it with the disciples, as here. Some older versions attach it to the warning.

text.q: Nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered, or hidden that will not be made known.
So whatever you have said in the dark will be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed on the housetops.
I tell you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do nothing more.
But I will show you whom to fear: fear the one who, after killing, has authority to throw into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear him.

verse.note: Gehenna is the Greek form of the Hebrew name for the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, which by this period had become a name for the place of final judgment. Most translations render it “hell”, usually with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept here because “hell” merges it with Hades and with later imagery.

text.q: Are not five sparrows sold for two copper coins? And not one of them is forgotten before God.

verse.note: The coin is the assarion, a copper coin worth one-sixteenth of a denarius, which was roughly a labourer's daily wage. Sparrows were among the cheapest food sold at market. The “penny” of verse 59 is a different coin, the lepton, the smallest in circulation and worth an eighth of an assarion.

text.q: But even the hairs of your head have all been counted. Do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before people, the Son of Man will also acknowledge before the angels of God;
but whoever denies me before people will be denied before the angels of God.
And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not worry about how or with what you will defend yourselves, or what you will say;
for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what must be said.”

verse.text: Someone from the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?”
Then he said to them, “Watch out, and guard yourselves against every kind of greed, because even when someone has plenty, his life does not come from his possessions.”
And he told them a parable: “The land of a certain rich man yielded a good harvest.

text.q: He reasoned to himself, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’
And he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods,
and I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself.”’

verse.note: The Greek word covers a person's life and self as well as “soul”. The rich man is simply addressing himself, and no contrast between soul and body is implied. The same word is translated “life” in verses 22 and 23, so that Jesus's teaching there picks up directly from the parable.

text.q: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This very night your soul is being demanded back from you. And what you have prepared, whose will it be?’
So it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

verse.text: Then he said to his disciples, “For this reason I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.

text.q: For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.
Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap; they have no storeroom or barn, yet God feeds them. How much more you are worth than the birds!
And which of you by worrying can add a cubit to his span of life?

verse.note: The Greek word can mean either age (length of life) or bodily height, and a cubit is a measure of length, about half a metre. Older translations have “add one cubit to his stature”. Most modern scholars prefer lifespan, since verse 26 calls the addition a very small thing, which a cubit of height would not be.

text.q: If then you cannot do even the smallest thing, why do you worry about the rest?
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin. But I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.
If God so clothes the grass, which is in the field today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith!
And you, do not seek what you will eat and what you will drink, and do not be anxious;
for all the nations of the world seek after these things, but your Father knows that you need them.

verse.note: The Greek word translated “nations” is the same word translated “Gentiles” elsewhere, since in the plural it often means the non-Jewish peoples. Here the full phrase “all the nations of the world” has the whole world in view. The parallel saying in Matthew 6:32 lacks “of the world” and is usually rendered “the Gentiles”.

text.q: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you.
Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.
Sell your possessions and give to the needy. Make for yourselves purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in the heavens, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed it.

text.q: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Have your belts fastened and your lamps burning,

verse.note: Literally “let your loins be girded”: a long robe was gathered up and tucked into the belt for work or travel, so the phrase means being dressed and ready to move. It echoes the Passover instructions in Exodus 12:11. The same verb returns in verse 37, where the master fastens his own belt to wait on his slaves.

text.q: and be like people waiting for their master to come back from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him at once.
Blessed are those slaves whom the master, when he comes, will find awake. Truly I tell you, he will fasten his belt, have them recline at table, and come and serve them.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired servant, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. Many English translations use “servants”, partly to avoid associations with modern race-based slavery. Several recent translations use “slaves”.

text.q: Whether he comes in the second watch or in the third, if he finds them so, blessed are they.
But know this: if the owner of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into.
You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.”

verse.text: Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone as well?”
And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and sensible manager whom the master will appoint over his household staff, to give them their food allowance at the proper time?

text.q: Blessed is that slave whom his master, when he comes, will find doing so.
I tell you truly, he will appoint him over all his possessions.
But if that slave says in his heart, ‘My master is taking a long time to come,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk,
the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two and assign him his place with the unfaithful.

verse.note: The verb literally means to cut in two, a punishment known in the ancient world. Because the slave is afterwards assigned a place, some interpreters take it as vivid language for severe punishment or for being cut off from the household. In the same verse “the unfaithful” could also be rendered “the unbelievers”.

text.q: That slave who knew his master’s will but did not prepare or act according to it will be beaten with many blows;

but the one who did not know it, and did things deserving blows, will be beaten with few. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required, and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be asked.
I came to throw fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!

note.term: how I wish it were already kindled
note.traditional: how I wish it were already kindled

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and difficult, literally “and what do I wish if it has already been kindled”. Most scholars read it as an exclamation of longing, as here. A minority read it as a question: “what more do I want, if it is already kindled?”

text.q: I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how hard pressed I am until it is completed!
Do you think that I have come to give peace on the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.
For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three;

they will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.”

note.term: father against son and son against father

verse.note: The list of divided family members echoes Micah 7:6, where the breakdown of trust within a household is a mark of a time of crisis before God acts. Hearers who knew the prophets would have recognised the allusion.

verse.text: He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A rainstorm is coming,’ and so it happens.

text.q: And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens.
Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you do not know how to interpret this present time?
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is just?

verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). Most translations have “what is right” here. “Just” is used because the saying leads straight into an illustration from a lawsuit, where a fair judgment is the point.

text.q: For as you are going with your opponent before a magistrate, make an effort on the way to settle with him, so that he does not drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the bailiff, and the bailiff throw you into prison.
I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid back even the last penny.”

verse.text: At that very time some people were present who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.

note.term: whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices

verse.note: The phrase means that Pilate's soldiers killed these Galilean pilgrims while they were offering sacrifice, presumably in the Jerusalem temple. No other ancient source records this incident, though it fits what is otherwise reported of Pilate's governorship. The collapse of the tower at Siloam in verse 4 is likewise known only from this passage.

verse.text: He answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they have suffered these things?

text.q: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish likewise.

verse.note: Most translations keep 'repent', an established term which readers are expected to understand as including a change of life. In current English, however, 'repent' centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. 'Turn back' is used for that reason.

text.q: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the other people living in Jerusalem?

verse.note: The Greek word is literally 'debtors'. Speaking of sin as a debt owed to God was an ordinary Jewish idiom of the period, as in the Lord's Prayer, so the word stands here as a simple parallel to 'sinners' in verse 2. The translation follows the usual English rendering, since 'debtors' alone would suggest money to a modern reader.

text.q: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish in the same way.”

verse.text: Then he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and found none.

text.q: So he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down! Why should it use up the ground as well?’
But he answered him, ‘Sir, leave it alone this year too, until I dig around it and put on manure.
Then if it bears fruit in the coming year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’”

verse.note: The Greek sentence breaks off after 'if it bears fruit in the coming year' and leaves the conclusion unspoken, a recognised idiom in which the hearer supplies 'so much the better'. English needs the words, and most translations add them as here.

verse.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.
And there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years; she was bent over and could not straighten up at all.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can go with 'could not', meaning she was wholly unable to straighten up, or with 'straighten up', meaning she could not straighten up fully. Translations are divided; the first reading is followed here.

verse.text: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are released from your infirmity,”
and he laid his hands on her. At once she was made straight, and she began to glorify God.

But the synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, responded by saying to the crowd, “There are six days on which work ought to be done. So come and be healed on those days, and not on the Sabbath day.”
The Lord answered him, “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath release his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to give it water?

text.q: And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen long years, ought she not to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

verse.text: As he said these things, all his opponents were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things that were being done by him.
So he said, “What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it?

text.q: It is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his own garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches.”

note.traditional: lodged / made nests in its branches

verse.note: The wording echoes Old Testament pictures of a great tree in whose branches the birds settle (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12, 21), an image for a kingdom that shelters many peoples. A hearer who knew those passages would catch more than a remark about garden plants.

verse.text: And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God?

text.q: It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

verse.note: The measure is the saton (Hebrew seah). Estimates of its size vary, but three of them come to something like twenty-five to forty litres of flour, enough bread for a very large gathering. The scale is part of the point: a small lump of leaven works through a huge batch.

verse.text: He went on through towns and villages, teaching and making his way to Jerusalem.
Someone said to him, “Lord, are those who are being saved few?” And he said to them,

text.q: “Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able,

once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us.’ And he will answer you, ‘I do not know you or where you are from.’

note.term: once the master of the house has risen
note.traditional: When once the master of the house has risen (beginning a new sentence)

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated in two ways. The edition translated here joins this clause to verse 24: many will be unable to enter once the door has been shut. Many translations instead put a full stop after verse 24 and begin a new sentence here, with its main clause either at 'he will answer you' or in verse 26.

text.q: Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’
And he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from. Get away from me, all you wrongdoers!’
There will be weeping there, and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves driven outside.
And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and will recline at table in the kingdom of God.
And look, there are last who will be first, and there are first who will be last.”

verse.text: At that very hour some Pharisees came up and said to him, “Leave and go on your way from here, because Herod wants to kill you.”
He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Look, I am driving out demons and accomplishing healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I reach my goal.’
verse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, who had executed John the Baptist. In Greek usage the fox stood for craftiness; in Jewish usage it could also stand for a petty figure as opposed to a lion. Either or both may be meant, and in any case the tone is contemptuous.

note.traditional: I shall be perfected / I finish my course

verse.note: The verb means to bring to completion, and the form can be read as 'I complete (my work)' or as a passive, 'I am brought to completion', that is, by God. Most interpreters see a veiled reference to Jesus' death and what follows it in Jerusalem, as verse 33 suggests. 'Today, tomorrow and the third day' is an idiom for a short, fixed span of time, though many hear an echo of the resurrection.

text.q: Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem.

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her! How often I wanted to gather your children the way a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you did not want it.
Look, your house is left to you. And I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

note.term: your house is left to you
note.traditional: your house is left unto you desolate

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'desolate', probably under the influence of Jeremiah 22:5 and the parallel in Matthew 23:38; the earliest witnesses to Luke lack it. Without the word the sense is that the house, whether the temple or the city, is abandoned to its people's own keeping. The closing quotation is from Psalm 118:26.

verse.text: One Sabbath, when he went to the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees to eat bread, they were watching him closely.
verse.note: To 'eat bread' is a Semitic way of saying 'have a meal'; it does not mean that only bread was served. The phrase is kept because the guest in verse 15 picks it up when he speaks of eating bread in the kingdom of God.

verse.text: And there in front of him was a man who had dropsy.
verse.note: Dropsy is the older English name for what is now called edema: visible swelling of the body caused by retained fluid, usually a symptom of serious underlying illness. The Greek word is a standard medical term of the period and occurs only here in the New Testament.

verse.text: Jesus responded by asking the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it permitted to heal on the Sabbath, or not?”
verse.note: The traditional 'lawyers' suggests courtroom advocates to a modern reader. These were specialists in interpreting the Law of Moses, the same group elsewhere called scribes. Many recent translations make a similar adjustment.

verse.text: But they kept silent. So he took hold of the man, cured him, and sent him on his way.
Then he said to them, “Which of you, if your son or your ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day?”
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'donkey' instead of 'son', and a few read 'sheep'; the King James Version follows the 'donkey' reading. 'Son' has strong early support and is the more surprising pairing, which copyists would be likely to smooth to match the familiar 'ox and donkey'. Most modern editions therefore adopt it.

verse.text: And they were not able to give any answer to this.
He told a parable to those who had been invited, when he noticed how they were choosing the places of honor. He said to them,

text.q: “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not recline in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited by him,

verse.note: At formal meals guests lay on couches arranged around the table, leaning on the left elbow. The couches were ranked, so where one reclined showed one's standing publicly. The 'place of honor' is literally the 'first couch'.

text.q: and the one who invited both you and him will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this man.’ Then in shame you will begin to take the last place.

But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who has invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor in the presence of all who are reclining at table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

verse.text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not ask your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, in case they also invite you in return and that becomes your repayment.

text.q: But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind,
and you will be blessed, because they have no way to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

verse.text: When one of those reclining at table with him heard this, he said to him, “Blessed is whoever will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”
But he said to him, “A man was giving a great dinner and invited many.

text.q: At the hour of the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, because it is now ready.’

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. 'Servant' is the long-standing English rendering, though several modern translations now use 'slave'. Ancient slavery was not based on race and differed in various ways from later Atlantic slavery, but the person was still property.

text.q: But they all alike began to excuse themselves. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. I ask you, consider me excused.’

verse.note: The Greek is a compressed idiom, literally 'from one', with a noun left unstated. It probably means 'unanimously' or 'with one voice', though 'all at once' is also possible. Either way the point is that every guest refused.

text.q: Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am on my way to try them out. I ask you, consider me excused.’
And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and so I cannot come.’

The slave came and reported this to his master. Then the owner of the house became angry and said to his slave, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in here the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame.’
And the slave said, ‘Master, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’
And the master said to the slave, ‘Go out to the roads and hedgerows and press them to come in, so that my house may be filled.

verse.note: The verb covers a range from physical force to insistent urging, and standard lexicons place this verse at the urging end: a single slave cannot force strangers into a house, and the picture is of overcoming polite reluctance. 'Compel' is the usual English rendering and is not wrong, but it suggests coercion. The verse was later cited to justify forced conversion, a reading the story does not support.

text.q: For I tell you, none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.’”

verse.note: 'You' is plural in Greek, although the master has been speaking to a single slave. The sentence is punctuated here as the close of the master's speech, as most translations do. It may instead be Jesus stepping outside the story to address the dinner guests directly, in which case 'my dinner' is his own.

verse.text: Large crowds were travelling with him, and he turned and said to them,

text.q: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own life as well, he cannot be my disciple.

verse.note: In Semitic idiom 'love' and 'hate' can express preference, not emotion: to 'hate' one thing is to put it second to another (compare Genesis 29:30–31 and the parallel in Matthew 10:37, 'loves father or mother more than me'). The stark wording is kept because it is what the Greek says. The demand is for overriding loyalty, not hostility toward one's family.

text.q: Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
For which of you, wanting to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?
Otherwise, once he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who are watching will begin to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
Or what king, going out to meet another king in battle, will not first sit down and consider whether he is strong enough with ten thousand to face the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
If he is not, then while the other is still far away he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
So then, any one of you who does not give up all that he has cannot be my disciple.
Salt, then, is good; but if even the salt loses its taste, with what will it be seasoned?

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means 'to make or become foolish'; applied to salt it means to become insipid. A Greek reader may have heard a hint of the disciple who becomes foolish. How salt could lose its saltiness is debated; impure salt from the Dead Sea region could have its true salt leached out, leaving a useless residue.

text.q: It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile; they throw it out. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verse.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him to listen to him.
And both the Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling, saying, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
So he told them this parable:

text.q: “What man among you, who has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the lost one until he finds it?
And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing,
and when he comes home he calls together his friends and neighbors and says to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’
I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who turns back than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of turning back.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repent' and 'repentance'. In modern English 'repent' centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

text.q: Or what woman who has ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search carefully until she finds it?

verse.note: The drachma was a Greek silver coin, roughly equal in value to the Roman denarius, which was about a day's wage for a labourer. Ten of them would be a modest household's savings, so losing one mattered.

text.q: And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors and says, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma that I lost.’
In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who turns back.”

verse.text: Then he said, “A man had two sons.

text.q: The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me.’ So he divided his livelihood between them.

note.term: the share of the property that falls to me
note.traditional: the portion of goods that falleth to me

verse.note: The phrase is ordinary legal language for the portion of an inheritance due to an heir. Under Deuteronomy 21:17 the firstborn received a double share, so the younger of two sons could expect a third. An inheritance normally passed at the father's death; asking for it while he was alive would have struck hearers as a serious affront.

text.q: Not many days later the younger son gathered everything together and went abroad to a distant country, and there he squandered his property by living recklessly.
When he had spent everything, a severe famine came over that country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs.

verse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the Jewish law (Leviticus 11:7), and tending them was regarded as degrading work for a Jew. For the original audience this detail marks how far the son has fallen, in a Gentile land and in Gentile service.

text.q: He longed to fill his belly with the carob pods the pigs were eating, and no one would give him anything.

note.traditional: fill his belly with / be fed with

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided here. Some read 'fill his belly with', which is the reading of the edition translated here; other early manuscripts read 'be satisfied with', which several modern editions and translations follow. The sense is little affected.

The Greek word means 'little horns' and refers to the curved pods of the carob tree, common around the Mediterranean. They were used as animal fodder and eaten by people only in poverty. The older English 'husks' is less exact.

text.q: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired workers have more than enough bread, while I am perishing here from hunger!

verse.note: The Greek verb here is the same one translated 'lose' and 'lost' throughout the chapter (the lost sheep, the lost coin, the son who 'was lost'). It covers both being lost and being destroyed, and a Greek reader would hear the son describing himself with the word that runs through all three parables.

text.q: I will get up and go to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight;

verse.note: 'Heaven' here is a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. The son is confessing that he has sinned against God and against his father.

text.q: I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers.”’
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion; he ran, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’

note.term: I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

verse.note: Some early manuscripts add 'Make me like one of your hired workers' at the end of this verse. Most editors regard the addition as copied from verse 19. On the shorter reading, the son does not finish his prepared speech before the father speaks.

text.q: But the father said to his slaves, ‘Quick! Bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.

verse.note: Most English versions have 'servants', though some recent ones have 'slaves'. The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, a person owned by the household. The parable distinguishes these from the 'hired workers' of verses 17 and 19, who were free day labourers. The older son's complaint in verse 29, 'I have been slaving for you', uses the related verb.

text.q: Bring the fattened calf and slaughter it, and let us eat and celebrate,
because this son of mine was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found.’ And they began to celebrate.
Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants over and asked what this might be.
He told him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because he has got him back safe and sound.’
But he became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and began pleading with him.

But he answered his father, ‘Look, all these years I have been slaving for you, and I have never disobeyed a command of yours; yet you have never given me even a young goat so that I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with prostitutes, you slaughtered the fattened calf for him!’
He said to him, ‘My child, you are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours.
But it was necessary to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’”

verse.text: He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was squandering his property.
verse.note: The Greek word names the person, often a slave or freedman, who ran an estate and its accounts on the owner's behalf. 'Steward' is the older English rendering, but the word now suggests a flight attendant or a ceremonial official. Most recent translations also use 'manager'.

text.q: So he called him and said, ‘What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig; I am ashamed to beg.
I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the management people will welcome me into their homes.’
So he summoned his master’s debtors one by one. He said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’
He said, ‘A hundred baths of olive oil.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’

verse.note: The bath (liquid) and the cor (dry, verse 7) are Hebrew units of measure. Their exact sizes in this period are uncertain: a bath was perhaps 20 to 40 litres and a cor perhaps 200 to 400 litres. On any reckoning these are large commercial debts, and the reductions are substantial.

text.q: Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill and write eighty.’
And the master praised the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light.

verse.note: The Greek word can mean the manager's master, as in verses 3 and 5, or 'the Lord', meaning Jesus. Most interpreters take it as the master inside the story, who admires the manager's shrewdness without approving of his dishonesty. A minority take it as Luke's report that Jesus commended the manager, which would end the parable at verse 7.

text.q: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth, so that when it fails they may welcome you into the eternal tents.

verse.note: Luke keeps the Aramaic word mamona, an ordinary term for money and property, which older translations carried over as 'mammon'. It is rendered 'wealth' here because 'Mammon' has since come to sound like the name of a demon; in verse 13 it is pictured as a rival master. 'Dishonest' renders 'of unrighteousness', the same phrase used of the manager in verse 8. Whether it means wealth gained dishonestly or wealth as belonging to this unjust age is disputed.

'They' may be the friends made by generous use of wealth, usually understood as the poor who have been helped. It may instead be an indefinite plural, a reverent Jewish way of saying 'God may welcome you'. The wording deliberately echoes the manager's hope in verse 4 of being welcomed into people's homes.

The Greek word ordinarily means a tent, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the tabernacle and the tents of the wilderness. Most translations generalise to 'dwellings' or 'homes'. 'Tents' is kept because the pairing of a tent with permanence is in the Greek. 'Eternal' here carries the Jewish sense of belonging to the age to come.

text.q: Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and whoever is dishonest in very little is dishonest also in much.
So if you have not been faithful with dishonest wealth, who will trust you with the true wealth?
And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?
No household slave can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and wealth.”

verse.text: The Pharisees, who loved money, were listening to all this, and they sneered at him.
And he said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves in the sight of people, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among people is an abomination in the sight of God.

text.q: The Law and the Prophets were until John. Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is being proclaimed, and everyone is forcing their way into it.

note.term: everyone is forcing their way into it

verse.note: The verb form can be middle ('forces a way in') or passive ('is forced' or 'is urgently pressed' to enter). Most translations take it as middle, as here, describing people pushing eagerly, or perhaps aggressively, into the kingdom. Some scholars prefer the passive: 'everyone is urged insistently to enter it'. The saying is compressed and its exact force remains disputed.

text.q: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter of the Law to fall.
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
There was a rich man who used to dress in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day.
And a poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gate, covered with sores
and longing to eat his fill of what fell from the rich man’s table. Instead, even the dogs would come and lick his sores.
In time the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried.

verse.note: The Greek word means the chest or lap, or the fold of a garment over it. The picture is probably of reclining next to Abraham as the guest of honour at a banquet, as in John 13:23, though some see a child held close. 'Bosom' is the traditional rendering and several recent translations use 'side'. The plural form in verse 23 has the same sense.

text.q: And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

verse.note: Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew Sheol. It is a different word from Gehenna, the place of final punishment, although in this story the rich man is already suffering there. The scene draws on popular Jewish pictures of the afterlife in which the dead await judgment in separate conditions.

text.q: He called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in agony in this flame.’
But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, and Lazarus likewise the bad; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.
And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’
He said, ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house,
for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, so that they too do not come to this place of torment.’
But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.’
He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will turn back.’

verse.note: 'Repent' in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, which is a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a changed life.

text.q: He said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

verse.text: He said to his disciples, “It is impossible for stumbling blocks not to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!

text.q: It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble.
Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he turns back, forgive him.

verse.note: The Greek verb describes a change of direction in mind and conduct, echoing the prophets’ call to return to God. ‘Repent’ in modern English centres on feeling sorry, which is narrower. Most translations keep ‘repent’ as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

text.q: And if he sins against you seven times in a day and seven times returns to you saying, ‘I turn back,’ you shall forgive him.”

verse.text: The apostles said to the Lord, “Give us more faith.”
The Lord said, “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.

text.q: Which of you who has a slave plowing or tending sheep will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at the table’?

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and the parable depends on this: the master owes him no thanks for his labour. Many translations use ‘servant’, which softens the picture; several recent ones use ‘slave’.

text.q: Will he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare something for my dinner, then fasten your belt and serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and after that you will eat and drink yourself’?
Does he thank the slave because he did what was ordered?
So you also, when you have done everything you were ordered, say, ‘We are unworthy slaves; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

verse.note: The word ordinarily means ‘useless’ or ‘worthless’, but these slaves have done all that was required of them, so it cannot be meant literally. Most interpreters take it as an expression of modesty: slaves with no claim to credit or reward. Some propose the sense ‘to whom nothing is owed’, though that meaning is not clearly attested elsewhere.

verse.text: As he was traveling to Jerusalem, he was passing between Samaria and Galilee.

note.traditional: through the midst of Samaria and Galilee

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean either ‘along the border between’ the two regions or ‘through the middle of’ both. The first is the more common view and fits a mixed group of Jews and a Samaritan. The order of the names, Samaria before Galilee, is odd for a journey south to Jerusalem on either reading.

verse.text: As he was entering a certain village, ten men with leprosy met him. They stood at a distance
verse.note: The Greek term covers a range of skin conditions, not only the disease now called leprosy. Under the Law of Moses (Leviticus 13–14) such conditions made a person ritually unclean and required living apart, which is why the men stand at a distance. A priest had to examine the person and declare them clean before they could return to the community, hence the instruction in verse 14.

verse.text: and raised their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they were going, they were made clean.
One of them, seeing that he had been healed, came back, glorifying God with a loud voice,
and fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, thanking him. And he was a Samaritan.
Jesus responded, “Were not the ten made clean? Where are the nine?

text.q: Was none of them found coming back to give glory to God except this foreigner?”
