verse.note: This word, literally ‘of another race’, occurs only here in the New Testament. It is the term used in the warning inscription in the Jerusalem temple that barred non-Jews from the inner courts. Jews and Samaritans regarded each other with hostility, which gives the point its edge.

verse.text: And he said to him, “Get up and go; your faith has saved you.”
verse.note: The Greek verb means both ‘heal’ and ‘rescue, save’. Most modern translations have ‘made you well’ here. But all ten were healed, and Luke uses different verbs for that in verses 14 and 15, so this word to the one who came back probably says something more. The verb is ambiguous and may carry both senses.

verse.text: Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God was coming, he answered them, “The kingdom of God does not come in a way that can be observed,

note.term: in a way that can be observed

verse.note: The Greek noun means close watching, as of symptoms or of the sky. The likeliest sense is that the kingdom’s arrival cannot be tracked or predicted by watching for signs. A minority take it as ‘with observance’ of religious rules.

text.q: nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ For look, the kingdom of God is among you.”

verse.note: The Greek preposition usually means ‘inside’, and older translations have ‘within you’. Most modern translations prefer ‘among you’ or ‘in your midst’. One reason is that Jesus is speaking to Pharisees; another is that Luke nowhere else describes the kingdom as an inner state. A third proposal, ‘within your reach’, has also been made. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: Then he said to the disciples, “Days will come when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.

text.q: They will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go off or chase after them.
For just as lightning flashes and shines from one end of the sky to the other, so the Son of Man will be in his day.
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
And just as it was in the days of Noah, so it will also be in the days of the Son of Man:
they were eating, drinking, marrying, being given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
It was the same in the days of Lot: they were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building;
but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all.
It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed.
On that day, the one who is on the roof, with his belongings in the house, must not come down to get them, and likewise the one in the field must not return to what is behind.
Remember Lot’s wife.
Whoever seeks to preserve their life will lose it, but whoever loses it will keep it alive.
I tell you, on that night there will be two on one bed: one will be taken and the other left.
There will be two women grinding together: one will be taken and the other left.”

note.term: one will be taken and the other left

verse.note: Verse 36 (‘Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left’) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here. It was probably added by copyists from the parallel in Matthew 24:40. The traditional verse numbering therefore passes from 35 to 37.

verse.text: And they answered him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the body is, there the vultures also will be gathered.”
verse.note: The Greek word normally means ‘eagle’ but was also used for vultures, and birds gathering at a body, here meaning a corpse, points to vultures. Most modern translations render it so. Some interpreters keep ‘eagles’ and see an allusion to the eagle standards of the Roman army. The saying is proverbial, and its exact point is debated.

verse.text: Then he told them a parable about their need to pray always and not lose heart,
saying, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected people.

text.q: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him, saying, ‘Give me justice against my opponent.’
For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Even though I neither fear God nor respect people,
yet because this widow keeps causing me trouble, I will give her justice, so that she does not wear me out with her endless coming.’”

verse.note: The verb literally means to strike someone under the eye, to give a black eye, and Paul uses it of a boxer's blows in 1 Corinthians 9:27. Most interpreters take it figuratively here, as in this rendering. Some think the judge is wryly afraid the widow will actually come and hit him, or that she will blacken his reputation. The phrase rendered 'endless' can also mean 'in the end'.

verse.text: And the Lord said, “Hear what the unjust judge says.

text.q: And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who cry out to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?

note.term: Will he delay long over them?
note.traditional: though he bear long with them; Will he delay long over them?

verse.note: This clause is one of the hardest in Luke. The verb normally means 'be patient', and the clause can be read as a second question expecting the answer no (as here, with most modern translations) or as a concession: 'even though he is patient with them', that is, even though he seems slow to act. Scholars remain divided.

text.q: I tell you, he will bring about justice for them quickly. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

verse.text: He also told this parable to some who were confident in themselves that they were righteous and who looked down on the rest:
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'righteous' here and 'justified' in verse 14 are the adjective and verb of the same root, so the man who goes home 'justified' is the one declared to be what the others assumed they were. 'Just' and 'vindicated' would be equally possible English. The widow's 'justice' and the 'unjust' judge in verses 3–8 use related words. 'Righteous' and 'justify' are the standard English renderings; most other languages use a single word for 'just' throughout.

text.q: “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed this to himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of people—robbers, wrongdoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.

note.traditional: stood and prayed thus with himself

verse.note: The Greek phrase 'to himself' can go with 'prayed' (he prayed silently, or perhaps about himself) or with 'stood' (he stood by himself, apart from others). Manuscripts vary in the word order, which reflects the same uncertainty. Many modern translations choose 'stood by himself and prayed'.

text.q: I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I acquire.’
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but kept beating his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner!’

verse.note: This is not the ordinary plea for mercy that the blind man uses in verse 38. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of atonement and sacrifice; its only other New Testament use is Hebrews 2:17, of making atonement for sins. Spoken in the temple, the prayer is close to 'let atonement be made for me'. The traditional rendering is kept as the most natural English.

The Greek has the definite article. Most translations treat it as generic and write 'a sinner', which is grammatically possible. Given its full force, it has the tax collector see himself as the sinner, in contrast to the Pharisee, who measures himself against other people.

text.q: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

verse.text: People were bringing even their babies to him so that he might touch them; but when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

verse.text: A certain ruler asked him, “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age', and in Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. Verse 30 makes the link explicit: 'in the coming age eternal life'. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators prefer 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one: God.

text.q: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not give false testimony, honor your father and mother.’”

verse.text: He said, “All these I have kept since my youth.”
When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens; then come, follow me.”
But when he heard this he became deeply grieved, for he was extremely rich.
Jesus looked at him and said, “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!

text.q: Indeed, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.note: The image is deliberately absurd: the largest animal familiar to the hearers and the smallest opening. The popular explanation that the 'Needle's Eye' was a narrow gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence behind it. The saying means what verse 27 says, that the thing is humanly impossible.

verse.text: Those who heard this said, “Then who can be saved?”
He said, “What is impossible with people is possible with God.”
Then Peter said, “Look, we have left what was ours and followed you.”
He said to them, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or sisters or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God
verse.note: The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to refer to siblings of both sexes. The parallel saying in Mark 10:29 spells out 'brothers or sisters'. Some translations keep 'brothers' here.

text.q: who will not receive back many times as much in this present time, and in the coming age eternal life.”

verse.text: Taking the twelve aside, he said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished.

text.q: For he will be handed over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and abused and spat upon,

verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples, and it is translated 'Gentiles' in that sense and 'nations' elsewhere. Here it refers to the Roman authorities.

text.q: and after flogging him they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”

verse.text: But they understood none of this; this saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was being said.
As he was approaching Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road begging.
Hearing a crowd going by, he asked what this was.
They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.”
And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be quiet; but he shouted all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and ordered him to be brought to him. When he came near, he asked him,
“What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me see again.”
And Jesus said to him, “See again; your faith has saved you.”

note.traditional: hath saved thee; has made you well

verse.note: The verb covers both rescue from illness or danger and salvation in the fuller sense. It is the same verb as in verse 26, 'Then who can be saved?'. Many translations write 'made you well' or 'healed you' here. 'Saved' keeps the link with verse 26 and leaves both senses open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: And at once he could see again, and he began following him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
He entered Jericho and was passing through it.
And look, there was a man named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short in stature.
So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree to see him, because Jesus was about to pass that way.
verse.note: The tree is the sycamore fig, a large fig species common in the Jordan valley, with low spreading branches that are easy to climb. It is unrelated to the trees called sycamore in Europe and North America.

verse.text: When he came to the place, Jesus looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
So he hurried down and welcomed him joyfully.
And all who saw it began to grumble, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man.”
But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I am giving to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I am paying it back fourfold.”
verse.note: The Greek verbs for giving and paying back are in the present tense. Most interpreters take them as a resolution made on the spot in response to Jesus (“I hereby give”). A minority read them as Zacchaeus describing his existing practice, in defence against the crowd's charge that he is a sinner. The rendering leaves both readings open, though Jesus' words about salvation coming “today” favour the first.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.

text.q: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.”

verse.text: As they were listening to these things, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.
So he said, “A man of noble birth travelled to a distant country to receive kingship for himself and then return.
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “kingdom” in verse 11, but here it means the royal title and power, since the man returns to rule his own country. First-century hearers knew the pattern. Local rulers travelled to Rome to be confirmed as king, and Josephus reports that when Herod's son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, a delegation from Judea followed to oppose him.

text.q: He called ten of his slaves, gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most older English versions soften it to “servants”, though several recent ones use “slaves”. Slaves in the ancient world were often entrusted with managing money and business for their owners.

A mina was a sum of money equal to one hundred drachmas, roughly three to four months' wages for a labourer. Each slave receives one mina. The amount is modest, which is why the king calls it “a very small thing” in verse 17.

text.q: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’

And it happened that when he returned, having received the kingship, he ordered those slaves to whom he had given the money to be called to him, so that he might learn what they had gained by doing business.
The first came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has earned ten minas more.’
And he said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you proved faithful in a very small thing, have authority over ten cities.’
The second came and said, ‘Your mina, Master, has made five minas.’
And he said to this one too, ‘And you, be over five cities.’
Then the other came and said, ‘Master, look, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth.
For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down and reap what you did not sow.’
He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked slave! You knew, did you, that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow?
Why then did you not put my money in the bank? And I, on my return, would have collected it with interest.’
And to those standing by he said, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’
And they said to him, ‘Master, he has ten minas!’
‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

verse.note: It is not certain whether verse 26 is spoken by the king inside the story or by Jesus stepping outside it to address his hearers. The translation treats it as the king's words, because verse 27 continues without a break in the king's voice. Verse 25 is an interruption by the bystanders, and a few ancient witnesses omit it.

text.q: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.’”

verse.text: Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
And it happened that as he came near Bethphage and Bethany, at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples,
saying, “Go into the village opposite, and as you enter it you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it.

text.q: And if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you are to say this: ‘The Lord needs it.’”

note.traditional: The Lord has need of it

verse.note: The Greek word for “Lord” here is the same word translated “owners” in verse 33, so there is a play between the colt's owners and the Lord who claims it. The words could also be construed as “Its master needs it.” Most translations read it as the text does here.

verse.text: Those who had been sent went off and found it just as he had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
They said, “The Lord needs it.”
And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.
As he went along, people were spreading their cloaks on the road.
As he was now drawing near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the deeds of power they had seen,
saying, “Blessed is the one who comes, the king, in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!”
verse.note: The acclamation quotes Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the festivals, with “the king” added. The second line echoes the angels' song at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:14), but here the peace is located in heaven.

verse.text: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”
He answered, “I tell you, if these keep silent, the stones will cry out.”
And as he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it,
saying, “If only you had recognized on this day, even you, the things that lead to peace! But now they have been hidden from your eyes.
verse.note: The Greek is a broken sentence, an “if” clause whose conclusion is never stated, as though the speaker were overcome. English versions either leave it unfinished or, as here, turn it into a wish. The verb is the same one translated “recognize” in verse 44.

text.q: For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a palisade against you and surround you and hem you in on every side,
and they will dash you to the ground, you and your children within you, and they will not leave stone upon stone in you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament, “visitation” is a set term for God coming to inspect his people, whether to rescue or to judge. The sense here is that God has come to Jerusalem in Jesus and the city has failed to recognize it. The siege language of verses 43–44 matches what the Roman army did to Jerusalem in AD 70.

verse.text: Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling,
saying to them, “It is written, ‘And my house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.”
verse.note: Jesus combines Isaiah 56:7 with Jeremiah 7:11, where the prophet warned that the temple would not protect those who treated it as a hideout. The Greek word means a violent robber or bandit, not a sneak thief, and the “den” is literally a cave where such men take refuge.

verse.text: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy him, and so were the leading men of the people,
but they could not find what they might do, for all the people hung on his words as they listened.
One day, as he was teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up with the elders,
and they said to him, “Tell us, by what authority are you doing these things? Or who is it that gave you this authority?”
He answered them, “I too will ask you a question, and you tell me:

text.q: Was John’s baptism from heaven or from human beings?”

verse.text: They reasoned it out among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’

text.q: But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

verse.text: So they answered that they did not know where it was from.
And Jesus said to them, “Nor am I telling you by what authority I am doing these things.”
Then he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and went abroad for a long time.

text.q: When the time came, he sent a slave to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Older English versions say 'servant'; several modern translations now use 'slave', as here. A landowner sending his slaves as agents was ordinary practice, and their mistreatment was an insult to the owner himself.

text.q: He went on to send another slave; but that one too they beat and humiliated and sent away empty-handed.
He went on to send a third; this one too they wounded and threw out.
Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’
But when the tenants saw him, they reasoned with one another, saying, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

verse.text: He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “May that never happen!”
But he looked straight at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 118:22, and the Greek is literally 'head of the corner'. It may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes it at the top; scholars are divided. Either way it is the most important stone, which the builders had thrown aside.

text.q: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; and anyone it falls on, it will crush.”

note.traditional: it will grind him to powder

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means to winnow, scattering chaff to the wind, so the sense may be 'it will scatter him like chaff'. In one Greek version of Daniel 2:44 it is used of a kingdom that crushes all others, in a passage about a stone, and most translators take that sense here.

verse.text: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him that very hour, but they feared the people; for they knew that he had told this parable against them.
So they watched him closely and sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in something he said and so hand him over to the rule and authority of the governor.
They questioned him, saying, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God.

text.q: Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”

verse.note: This was the direct tax Rome levied on subject peoples, imposed on Judea when it came under a Roman governor. Its introduction had provoked an uprising, and it remained a bitter issue. A plain yes would discredit Jesus with the people, and a plain no could be reported to the governor as sedition.

verse.text: But he saw through their craftiness and said to them,
“Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?” They answered, “Caesar’s.”
verse.note: A Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. It carried the emperor's portrait and titles, which under Tiberius included the claim to be son of the divine Augustus. Many Jews found such coins offensive, since they bore both an image and a claim to divinity.

verse.text: He said to them, “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
verse.note: The questioners asked whether it is lawful to 'give' tribute; Jesus answers with a compound of the same verb that means to give back or pay what is owed. 'Render' in the traditional versions meant this but no longer conveys it. The change of verb implies that the coin already belongs to Caesar, and leaves open what belongs to God.

verse.text: And they were unable to catch him in what he said in front of the people; and, amazed at his answer, they fell silent.
Then some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, came up and questioned him,
saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

note.term: raise up offspring for his brother
note.traditional: raise up seed unto his brother

verse.note: The reference is to the law in Deuteronomy 25:5–6, under which a dead man's brother married the widow and the first son counted as the dead man's heir. The Sadducees use it to make resurrection look absurd.

text.q: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless;
then the second
and the third took her, and in the same way all seven left no children and died.
Last of all, the woman died too.
So in the resurrection, whose wife does the woman become? For all seven had her as wife.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,

note.traditional: children of this world / sons of this age

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'sons of this age', a Semitic idiom in which 'son of' means 'belonging to'. The same idiom lies behind 'children of God' and 'children of the resurrection' in verse 36. 'This age' and 'that age' reflect the Jewish division of time into the present age and the age to come.

text.q: but those who are counted worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.
For they can no longer die either, because they are equal to angels, and they are children of God, being children of the resurrection.
But that the dead are raised, even Moses made known in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.

note.term: in the passage about the bush

verse.note: The Greek says only 'at the bush'. Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by naming its subject; this is the story of the burning bush in Exodus 3. The Sadducees accepted the books of Moses as authoritative, so Jesus argues from them.

text.q: He is not God of the dead but of the living, for to him all are alive.”

verse.note: The Greek is a bare dative, 'all live to him'. It may mean that from God's standpoint all are alive, as rendered here, or that all live for him or by his power. The argument is that God would not name himself as the God of people who had ceased to exist.

verse.text: Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.”
For they no longer dared to ask him anything.
Then he said to them, “How is it that they say the Messiah is David’s son?
verse.note: The Greek christos means 'anointed' and translates the Hebrew word that gives English 'Messiah', the title of the king Israel expected. Here the title itself is under discussion, so it is rendered 'Messiah'; where the word functions as a name for Jesus, this translation keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: For David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand

note.term: The Lord said to my Lord
note.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. The Hebrew has two different words, the divine name and 'my lord', a term for a superior; the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus' question turns on the second: David, the supposed speaker, calls the Messiah his lord, which a father would not normally say of his son.

text.q: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’
So David calls him ‘Lord’; how then is he his son?”

verse.text: While all the people were listening, he said to the disciples,

text.q: “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at dinners,
who devour widows’ houses and for show make long prayers. These will receive a heavier judgment.”

verse.text: Looking up, he saw rich people putting their gifts into the treasury.
He also saw a needy widow putting in two small copper coins,
verse.note: The lepton was the smallest coin in circulation in Judea, a tiny fraction of a labourer's daily wage. Two of them would buy almost nothing. The point of the scene is that they were all she had.

verse.text: and he said, “In truth I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them;

text.q: for all of these added to the gifts out of their surplus, but she, out of her need, put in everything she had to live on.”

verse.text: As some were speaking about the temple, how it was adorned with beautiful stones and dedicated offerings, he said,

text.q: “As for these things you are looking at, days will come when not a stone will be left on a stone that will not be torn down.”

verse.text: They asked him, “Teacher, when then will these things be, and what will be the sign when they are about to happen?”
He said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and, ‘The time has drawn near.’ Do not go after them.
verse.note: The Greek is simply ‘I am’ (egō eimi). Most translations supply ‘he’ and take it as a claim to be the Messiah, as the parallel in Matthew 24:5 spells out. Some hear an echo of God's self-declaration in the Greek Scriptures; that is possible but cannot be shown.

text.q: And when you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified; for these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once.”

verse.text: Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom;
verse.note: One Greek word, ethnos, lies behind ‘nation’ here, ‘all the nations’ and ‘Gentiles’ in verse 24, and ‘nations’ in verse 25. It means a people; in the plural it was also the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. English translations regularly divide it by sense in this way, but in verse 24 the nations to which captives are taken and the Gentiles who trample Jerusalem are the same word.

text.q: there will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and plagues, and there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.

But before all these things they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be led away before kings and governors for the sake of my name.
It will lead to your giving testimony.

note.term: It will lead to your giving testimony
note.traditional: it shall turn to you for a testimony

verse.note: The Greek says literally ‘it will turn out for you into testimony’. Most interpreters take this to mean that arrest and trial will become the disciples' occasion to bear witness, and the translation follows that view. It could also mean that the outcome will stand as testimony in the disciples' favour.

text.q: So settle it in your hearts not to rehearse your defense beforehand,
for I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand or contradict.
You will be handed over even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death,
and you will be hated by everyone because of my name.
Yet not a single hair of your head will perish.
By your endurance gain your lives.

note.traditional: you will gain your lives / possess ye your souls

verse.note: The text translated here has a command, ‘gain’; many manuscripts have a future, ‘you will gain’, and many English versions render it as a promise. The word translated ‘lives’ (psychē) is traditionally ‘souls’. It means a person's life or self, and here it refers to a life that survives even the death foretold in verse 16.

text.q: But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has drawn near.

verse.note: Roman armies besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the city and its temple in AD 70. Where Mark 13:14 and Matthew 24:15 speak of ‘the abomination of desolation’, Luke speaks plainly of armies and keeps the word ‘desolation’.

text.q: Then those in Judea must flee to the mountains, those inside the city must get out, and those in the countryside must not enter it,
because these are days of retribution, so that all that is written may be fulfilled.

verse.note: The Greek word means the exacting of justice or punishment, without the note of personal spite that ‘vengeance’ can carry in modern English. The phrase echoes the Greek Old Testament, where the prophets speak of the days of God's punishment (for example Hosea 9:7). Many versions still use ‘vengeance’.

text.q: Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days! For there will be great distress on the land and wrath against this people,

note.traditional: in the land / upon the earth

verse.note: The Greek word means both ‘land’ and ‘earth’, and translations are divided here. Because the next phrase speaks of ‘this people’ and the subject is Jerusalem and Judea, the land of Israel is the more likely meaning. In verse 25, where it is set against sun, moon and stars, the same word is rendered ‘earth’.

text.q: and they will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive into all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth nations in anguish, at a loss before the roar of the sea and its surging,
people fainting from fear and foreboding at what is coming upon the inhabited world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

verse.note: This is not the usual word for ‘world’ (kosmos) but oikoumenē, the inhabited earth, the world of human society. In ordinary usage it often meant in practice the Roman world, as in Luke 2:1. Most translations render it simply ‘the world’.

note.traditional: the powers of heaven / of the heavens

verse.note: The Greek is plural, and the plural is kept. The phrase draws on the language of the prophets (compare Isaiah 34:4) and refers to the heavenly host: sun, moon and stars, which ancient readers commonly associated with heavenly beings. Their shaking signals the undoing of the established order of the cosmos.

text.q: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.
When these things begin to happen, stand up straight and lift your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

verse.text: And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees.

text.q: When they are already putting out leaves, you see it and know for yourselves that summer is already near.
So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until everything has happened.

verse.note: The natural sense of the Greek is the people alive at the time of speaking, and many scholars take it so, referring ‘everything’ chiefly to the fall of Jerusalem. Others have understood it as the generation that sees the final signs, or more broadly as the Jewish people or humankind. The meaning is disputed, and the translation leaves the wording as it stands.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But be on your guard, or your hearts may be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the worries of daily life, and that day may come upon you suddenly
like a trap. For it will come upon all who live on the face of the whole earth.

note.traditional: For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell

verse.note: Manuscripts differ on where the sentence divides. In the text translated here, ‘like a trap’ completes verse 34: the day springs on the unwary like a trap. In many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, the words begin the next sentence: ‘for like a trap it will come upon all’.

text.q: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have the strength to escape all these things that are about to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

verse.text: During the days he was teaching in the temple, but at night he would go out and spend the night on the hill called the Mount of Olives.
And all the people would come to him early in the morning in the temple to listen to him.
Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, was drawing near.
And the chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to do away with him, for they were afraid of the people.
Then Satan entered Judas, the one called Iscariot, who belonged to the number of the Twelve.
He went off and discussed with the chief priests and the officers of the guard how he might hand him over to them.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to hand someone or something over, and is the ordinary word for delivering a person into custody. It does not in itself carry the idea of treachery, though the context supplies it here. Most English versions say “betray” for Judas’s act; this translation keeps “hand over” throughout the chapter (verses 4, 6, 21, 22, 48), so that the reader sees the same word that is used elsewhere of Jesus being handed over to the authorities.

verse.text: They were delighted and agreed to give him money.
He consented, and began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over to them when no crowd was present.
Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed.
Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, so that we may eat it.”
They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare it?”
He said to them, “Look, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters,

text.q: and say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you: “Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’
And he will show you a large upstairs room, furnished. Prepare it there.”

verse.text: They went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
And he said to them, “I have earnestly longed to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.

text.q: For I tell you, I will certainly not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: Then he took a cup, gave thanks and said, “Take this and share it among yourselves.

text.q: For I tell you, from now on I will certainly not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.”

verse.text: And he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body [which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

note.term: [which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

verse.note: The words in square brackets, running from here to the end of verse 20, are missing from one important early Greek manuscript and from several Old Latin copies, which therefore have no cup after the bread. They are present in almost all other manuscripts, including the earliest. Most scholars today regard them as original, but the edition translated here brackets them to mark the doubt.

verse.text: And he did the same with the cup after the supper, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”]

text.q: “But look, the hand of the one who is handing me over is with me on the table.
For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is handed over!”

verse.text: And they began to ask one another which of them it could be who was going to do this.
A dispute also arose among them as to which of them was considered the greatest.
But he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called Benefactors.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations” and, in the plural on Jewish lips, the non-Jewish peoples. The phrase could equally be translated “the kings of the nations”. English uses two words where the Greek has one.

“Benefactor” was a formal title of honour in the Greek-speaking world. It was voted to kings and wealthy patrons by the cities they favoured, and some Hellenistic kings bore it as part of their name. Jesus’ remark is pointed: rulers who dominate their subjects are publicly praised as their benefactors.

text.q: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
For who is greater, the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as the one who serves.
You are the ones who have stayed with me through my times of testing.
And I confer on you a kingdom, just as my Father conferred one on me,
so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
Simon, Simon, look! Satan has demanded to have all of you, to sift you like wheat,
but I have pleaded for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

verse.text: But he said to him, “Lord, with you I am ready to go both to prison and to death.”
He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have three times denied that you know me.”
And he said to them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.”
He said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever does not have a sword should sell his cloak and buy one.

note.term: whoever does not have a sword

verse.note: The Greek says only “the one who does not have”, without stating the object. It may mean “whoever has no sword”, as here and in most translations, or “whoever has no purse”, meaning that even someone without money should sell his cloak to buy a sword. Either way, most interpreters take the saying as a vivid warning of coming hostility, not as a literal instruction to arm.

text.q: For I tell you, this that is written must be brought to completion in me: ‘And he was counted among the lawless.’ For indeed what concerns me is reaching its completion.”

verse.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 53:12, part of the passage about the suffering servant. Jesus applies it to his coming arrest and execution alongside criminals. “Brought to completion” and “reaching its completion” reflect two related Greek words in the verse.

verse.text: They said, “Lord, look, here are two swords.” He said to them, “That is enough.”
verse.note: The reply can mean that two swords are sufficient, or it can be a way of closing the conversation, as in “Enough of this.” Most interpreters prefer the second, since the disciples have taken the saying about swords literally and Jesus later stops their use of one (verse 51). The translation leaves both readings open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: He went out and made his way, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him.
When he reached the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into testing.”
verse.note: The Greek word covers both a test or trial of someone’s loyalty and an enticement to do wrong; English “temptation” now suggests only the second. Here, on the night of the arrest, the danger is a crisis that will test the disciples’ loyalty, and the same word in verse 28 (“times of testing”) describes what Jesus himself has been through. Some modern versions likewise have “the time of trial”.

verse.text: And he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, knelt down and prayed,
saying, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me. Yet not my will but yours be done.”
And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.

note.term: an angel from heaven appeared to him

verse.note: Verses 43 and 44 are absent from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts and present in others, and they were known to Christian writers as early as the second century. Scholars are divided on whether Luke wrote them or they are a very early addition. The edition translated here prints them as part of the text.

verse.text: And being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.
When he rose from prayer and came to the disciples, he found them asleep from grief,
and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Get up and pray, so that you may not enter into testing.”
While he was still speaking, a crowd appeared, and the one called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He came up to Jesus to kiss him.
But Jesus said to him, “Judas, is it with a kiss that you hand over the Son of Man?”
When those around him saw what was about to happen, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”
And one of them struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his right ear.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee. “Servant” is the traditional English rendering, but it suggests a freer status than the word conveyed to a first-century reader. Many recent translations also use “slave”.

verse.text: But Jesus answered, “Stop! No more of this.” And he touched the ear and healed him.
verse.note: The Greek is terse, literally “Allow as far as this.” It is usually taken as a command to the disciples to stop fighting. It could also mean “Let them do even this”, that is, allow the arrest to go ahead. The translation follows the majority view.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to the chief priests, officers of the temple guard and elders who had come out against him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as if against a bandit?
verse.note: The word refers to someone who robs with violence, a brigand or outlaw, and not to a sneak thief, for which Greek has a different word. In the period it was also applied to armed insurgents. The point is that they have come armed as if he were a dangerous outlaw.

text.q: Day after day I was with you in the temple, and you did not lay a hand on me. But this is your hour, and the authority of darkness.”

verse.text: They seized him, led him away and brought him into the high priest’s house. Peter was following at a distance.
When they had lit a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat among them.
A slave girl saw him sitting in the firelight, looked closely at him and said, “This man was with him too.”
But he denied it, saying, “I do not know him, woman.”
A little later someone else saw him and said, “You are one of them too.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not!”
About an hour later another man kept insisting, “Certainly this man was with him too, for he is a Galilean.”
But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.
And the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before a rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.”
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
The men who were holding Jesus began mocking him and beating him.
They blindfolded him and kept asking, “Prophesy! Who is it that hit you?”
And they said many other abusive things against him.
When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered, both chief priests and scribes, and they brought him before their council,
saying, “If you are the Messiah, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will certainly not believe,
verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed one” and translates the Hebrew title for the king Israel expected. Here the council is asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, keeping “Christ” where the word functions as a name for Jesus.

text.q: and if I ask a question, you will certainly not answer.
But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”

verse.text: They all said, “Are you, then, the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say that I am.”
verse.note: The reply is indirect. It may be an idiom of assent (“You are right to say that I am”), or it may put the responsibility for the statement back on the questioners without a plain yes. The Greek could also be read “You say it, because I am.” The council treats it as an admission in the next verse.

verse.text: They said, “What further need do we have of testimony? We have heard it ourselves from his own mouth.”
Then the whole assembly of them rose and brought him before Pilate.
They began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man leading our nation astray, forbidding people to pay taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Messiah, a king.”
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one that, in the plural, is usually translated “Gentiles” when it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In the singular and used of Israel, as here, it simply means a people or nation. Dividing the word by sense in this way is standard practice.

The Greek word means “anointed” and was the title of the king Israel expected. Where the title itself is the point, as in this accusation, the translation uses “Messiah” and keeps “Christ” where the word works as a name; several modern translations make the same split. The phrase could also be read “an anointed king.” Either way the charge is framed so that a Roman governor would hear a rival to Caesar.

verse.text: Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”
Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no ground for a charge in this man.”
But they kept insisting, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, starting from Galilee and all the way to here.”
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean,
and on learning that he came under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself also in Jerusalem in those days.
When Herod saw Jesus he was very glad, for he had been wanting to see him for a considerable time because of what he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him.
He questioned him at considerable length, but Jesus gave him no answer.
The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him.
Herod too, with his troops, treated him with contempt and mocked him; then, putting a splendid robe on him, he sent him back to Pilate.
That very day Herod and Pilate became friends with each other; before this they had been at enmity.
Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,
and said to them, “You brought this man to me as one who was turning the people to revolt. Look, I examined him in your presence and found in this man no ground for the charges you bring against him.

text.q: Nor did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, he has done nothing deserving death.
So I will discipline him and release him.”

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means to train or correct a child. In a governor’s mouth it is a mild word for a beating given as a warning before release, and some translations say outright “have him flogged.” The rendering keeps Pilate’s understated term; the same word recurs in verse 22.

verse.text: But they all cried out together, “Away with this man! Release Barabbas for us!”
verse.note: There is no verse 17 in the Greek text translated here. The words “Now he was obliged to release one prisoner to them at the festival” are missing from the earliest manuscripts and appear at different places in others. They are generally regarded as a later explanatory addition drawn from the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark.

verse.text: This was a man who had been thrown into prison because of an uprising that had taken place in the city, and for murder.
Pilate addressed them again, wanting to release Jesus,
but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!”
A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has this man done? I have found in him no ground for a death sentence. So I will discipline him and release him.”
But they kept pressing him with loud voices, asking that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed.
So Pilate ruled that their request should be granted.
He released the man they asked for, the one who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, and Jesus he handed over to their will.
As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A great number of the people followed him, and among them women who were mourning and lamenting for him.
But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep rather for yourselves and for your children,

text.q: for look, days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never gave birth and the breasts that never nursed.’
Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

verse.note: The saying is proverbial; literally, “if they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” The usual understanding is that if such a fate falls on one who is innocent, like green wood that resists fire, far worse awaits a city ripe for judgment. Who “they” are is not stated and is disputed.

verse.text: Two others, criminals, were also being led away to be put to death with him.
When they came to the place called the Skull, they crucified him there, along with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verse.note: Luke gives only the Greek name of the place and omits the Aramaic name Golgotha that the other Gospels record. The familiar “Calvary” comes from the Latin word for skull used in the Latin Bible. Why the place had this name is not known.

verse.text: And Jesus was saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they cast lots to divide his clothes among them.

note.term: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

verse.note: This prayer is absent from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts and present in others of comparable age. Scholars are divided on whether Luke wrote it and some copyists removed it, or whether it is a very early tradition added to the Gospel. It is translated here as part of the text, as in the Greek edition followed.

verse.text: The people stood watching. The rulers too were sneering at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Messiah of God, the Chosen One.”
The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine
and saying, “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!”
There was also an inscription over him: “This is the King of the Jews.”
One of the criminals hanging there kept insulting him: “Are you not the Messiah? Save yourself and us!”
But the other answered, rebuking him, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence?

text.q: And we justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.”

verse.text: And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingdom.”

note.term: when you come in your kingdom
note.traditional: when you come into your kingdom

verse.note: Manuscripts divide between “into your kingdom” and “in your kingdom”; the Greek edition translated here prints the second. “In your kingdom” most naturally means “when you come as king,” looking to a future arrival in royal power, though the Greek preposition can also be used loosely for “into.” On the first reading, Jesus’s “today” in the next verse answers a request about the distant future with something immediate.

verse.text: He said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

note.term: today you will be with me
note.traditional: To day shalt thou be with me

verse.note: Ancient Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so “today” could in principle go with “I tell you” (“Truly I tell you today, you will be with me”). Nearly all scholars take it with what follows. “Truly I tell you” is a fixed formula that nowhere else takes a time word, and “today” answers the criminal’s “when.”

verse.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about midday and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated “land” can also mean “earth”; the Greek does not settle whether the darkness is local or universal.

verse.text: as the sun’s light failed; and the curtain of the temple was torn down the middle.
verse.note: The verb means to fail or give out and was also the ordinary term for an eclipse. An astronomical solar eclipse cannot occur at Passover, which falls at full moon, so the rendering does not specify one. Many later manuscripts read instead “and the sun was darkened,” which is the basis of the traditional wording.

verse.text: Then Jesus called out with a loud voice, “Father, into your hands I entrust my spirit.” Having said this, he breathed his last.
When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying, “Surely this man was righteous.”
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just), and this adjective can also mean “innocent.” After Pilate’s repeated findings of no guilt, “innocent” is at least part of the sense here, and many modern translations use it. “Righteous” is kept because Luke uses the same word of Joseph in verse 50 and, in Acts, calls Jesus “the Righteous One.”

verse.text: And all the crowds who had gathered for this spectacle, after watching what took place, returned beating their breasts.
All who knew him were standing at a distance, and so were the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things.
Now there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man—
he had not agreed with their decision and their action—from Arimathea, a town of the Jews, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God.
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
He took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.
It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.
verse.note: “Preparation” was the usual name for Friday, the day on which everything was made ready for the Sabbath. The Sabbath began at sunset, which is why the burial is hurried and the women wait. The Greek verb translated “was about to begin” literally means “was dawning,” used here loosely of the day’s onset in the evening.

verse.text: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid.
Then they returned and prepared spices and perfumed oils. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,
but when they went in they did not find the body.
While they were at a loss about this, suddenly two men in dazzling clothing stood beside them.
The women were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground, but the men said to them, “Why are you looking for the living one among the dead?

text.q: He is not here; he has been raised. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee,

verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either ‘he was raised’ (by God) or simply ‘he rose’. The passive is chosen here and in verse 34 because Luke elsewhere speaks of God raising Jesus, but many translations render it ‘he has risen’, and the grammar does not settle the question.

text.q: that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful people, and be crucified, and on the third day rise.”

verse.text: And they remembered his words,
and returning from the tomb they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
The women were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the others with them; they kept telling the apostles these things.
But to them these words seemed like nonsense, and they did not believe the women.
Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths and nothing else, and he went home, marveling at what had happened.
verse.note: The Greek phrase ‘to himself’ can go with ‘went away’ (to his own place, that is, home) or with ‘marveling’ (wondering to himself). Most modern translations take it as ‘went home’. The whole verse is absent from a small group of ‘Western’ manuscripts, but it is present in the great majority, including the earliest.

verse.text: Now on that same day two of them were on their way to a village named Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem,
verse.note: A stadion was a Greek measure of roughly 185 metres, so sixty stadia is about eleven kilometres or seven miles, a walk of two to three hours. The location of Emmaus is disputed.

verse.text: and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
While they were talking and debating, Jesus himself came near and began walking with them,
but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are these words you are exchanging with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, their faces downcast.
One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days?”
He said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet, powerful in deed and word before God and all the people,

text.q: and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
But we were hoping that he was the one who was going to set Israel free. And yet, on top of all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

verse.note: The verb means to release by payment or, more broadly, to liberate; the Greek Old Testament uses it for God bringing Israel out of Egypt. ‘Redeem’ is the traditional rendering and is accurate, but it now suggests personal salvation from sin, whereas the speakers are describing their hope for the nation's deliverance. Most translations keep ‘redeem’.

text.q: Moreover, some women of our group astounded us. They were at the tomb early in the morning
and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive.
Some of those with us went off to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “How foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!

text.q: Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”

verse.note: The Greek christos, ‘anointed one’, is here a title for the king Israel expected and not a name, and the point at issue is what that figure had to undergo. ‘Messiah’ makes the title audible; ‘Christ’ is kept in this translation where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explained to them the things about himself in all the Scriptures.
They drew near the village to which they were going, and he acted as though he were going farther.
But they pressed him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is already far gone.” So he went in to stay with them.
When he had reclined at the table with them, he took the bread and said the blessing, then broke it and began handing it to them.
verse.note: The Greek has no object: ‘he blessed’. At a Jewish meal the blessing over bread was a short prayer of praise addressed to God, not a consecration of the food, so ‘said the blessing’ reflects what a first-century reader would picture. The same verb is used in verses 50–53 for Jesus blessing the disciples and the disciples blessing God.

verse.text: Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him, and he vanished from their sight.
They said to each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as he spoke to us on the road, as he opened the Scriptures to us?”
They got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem, and they found the eleven and those with them gathered together,
who were saying, “The Lord really has been raised, and has appeared to Simon!”
Then they themselves related what had happened on the road, and how he was made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
While they were saying these things, he himself stood among them.
verse.note: Most manuscripts, including the earliest, continue ‘and said to them, “Peace to you.”’ The SBLGNT follows a small group of ‘Western’ witnesses that lack the words, judging them to have been added from John 20:19; most modern translations include them. The same edition follows a similar shorter reading at verse 3, where most manuscripts have ‘the body of the Lord Jesus’.

verse.text: Startled and terrified, they thought they were seeing a ghost.
verse.note: The Greek word is pneuma, the ordinary word for ‘spirit’. Here and in verse 39 it means the disembodied spirit of a dead person, which is what ‘ghost’ means in modern English. Older versions have ‘spirit’; several recent ones have ‘ghost’.

verse.text: He said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why are doubts rising in your hearts?

text.q: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”

verse.text: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]

note.term: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]

verse.note: The brackets reproduce those of the SBLGNT and mark the verse as doubtful. It is missing from a small group of ‘Western’ witnesses (one Greek manuscript and some early Latin and Syriac versions) and closely resembles John 20:20, which leads some scholars to regard it as a later addition. It is present in nearly all other manuscripts, including the earliest, and most modern editions and translations accept it.

verse.text: While they still could not believe it for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
They handed him a piece of broiled fish,
and he took it and ate it in front of them.
Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
and he said to them, “So it is written: the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day,

text.q: and turning back and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

verse.note: The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct; ‘repentance’ now tends to suggest mainly feeling sorry. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term understood to include a changed life. Some important manuscripts read ‘turning back for the forgiveness of sins’ in place of ‘and forgiveness’.

The Greek word here is the same one translated ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation; in the plural it can mean the non-Jewish peoples specifically or the peoples of the world generally. ‘Nations’ is used here because the scope is the whole world, starting from Jerusalem.

text.q: You are witnesses of these things.
And look, I am sending upon you what my Father promised. But you, stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

verse.text: Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them.
While he was blessing them, he parted from them [and was carried up into heaven].
verse.note: The brackets here and around ‘worshiped him and’ in verse 52 reproduce those of the SBLGNT and mark the words as doubtful. Both phrases are absent from a few ‘Western’ witnesses, and the first also from the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus. They are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including the earliest papyrus of Luke. Scholars are divided on whether they were added to make the ascension explicit or dropped to ease the comparison with Acts 1; most modern translations include them.

verse.text: And they [worshiped him and] returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
and they were continually in the temple, blessing God.
